title: Trump suggests letting Iran "take out" LA, San Diego during rally
summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom called President Trump "deranged and dangerous" after he suggested letting Iran "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom rebuked President Trump after he appeared to suggest letting Iran "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego if the country developed a nuclear weapon.

At a campaign rally in Nebraska, Mr. Trump said the Iran war is "artificial," but he wanted to see a "total victory." He suggested the war is a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."

"It's a little bit high," the president appeared to say about gas prices. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego."

Attendees appeared to cheer after his suggestion. It was not immediately clear what Mr. Trump meant, although the White House's rapid response account on X insisted after the fact that the president's words were being misinterpreted.
"He was saying the U.S. is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account said.
The comments were quickly condemned by Newsom and other California officials.

"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," Newsom wrote on X. "He is deranged and dangerous."

"I am directing the State Threat Assessment Center to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the president's remarks as an invitation to target California," Newsom added.
White House spokesperson Steven Cheung posted on X on Tuesday that "the media freakout" over Mr. Trump's remarks is "not rooted in reality."

"He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung continued. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."
Mr. Trump also suggested the war in Iran "will end very quickly, one way or the other, very soon."
In a statement to CBS News, Newsom then called for Mr. Trump to be removed from office under the 25th Amendment of the Constitution.
"Donald Trump is mentally ill. TIME FOR THE 25TH!" Newsom wrote.

In addition to being the country's second-most populous city, LA is home to the U.S. Space Force's Space Systems Command Headquarters, aerospace contractors including Lockheed Martin, Boeing and Northrop Grumman, and federally funded research centers such as the RAND Corporation.
"The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives," LA Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X.

At an event on Tuesday morning, Bass was asked by reporters her initial reaction to the president's comments. She said she was shocked and added: "Maybe at this point I shouldn't be, but I was just shocked."
"That's a president of the United States, inviting a country that we are at war with to attack an American city," Bass told reporters.
San Diego, the nation's eighth-largest city, has major military installations in and around it, including:

Naval Base San Diego, the homeport of the U.S. Navy's Pacific FleetMarine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, where 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members live and workNaval Amphibious Base Coronado, the main training ground for Navy SEALs on the West Coast
Naval Base San Diego, the homeport of the U.S. Navy's Pacific Fleet
Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, where 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members live and work
Naval Amphibious Base Coronado, the main training ground for Navy SEALs on the West Coast
"San Diego is not collateral damage," San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote on X. "We are not expendable. And we are never a 'small price to pay.' Keep our city out of your reckless war talk."

title: 2026 midterm election races to watch
summary: CBS News has identified 10 key Senate and 42 House races that will likely decide the majority — all of which can change during the midterm campaign.
story: CBS News' Battleground Tracker polling is back for 2026, capturing what's on voters' minds and the key groups to watch coast to coast, as well as what it means for districts, seat estimates and control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
Every district and state matters, but CBS News also identifies 10 key Senate and 42 House races that will likely decide the majority — all of which can change as the campaign rolls on.
Democrats and Republicans are focusing on a small number of races in the House and the Senate as they fight for control of Congress in the midterm elections this fall.
Republicans, who currently have the majority in both chambers, are vulnerable primarily because of the unpopular Iran war and continuing cost-of-living economic pressure.
Senate

Republicans have 53 seats, and Democrats have 47. Most of the 22 seats the GOP is defending are in states Mr. Trump easily won in 2024. Democrats must add a net total of four seats to take the majority while also defending a few seats against GOP challenges.
Here are the ten 2026 Senate races to watch:
Alaska

GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola are the front-runners in Alaska's top-four primary, where another candidate by the same name as the incumbent is also on the ballot. Alaska hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, but the party is eyeing the race as a pickup opportunity.
Iowa

GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek are facing off in Iowa after Sen. Joni Ernst decided not to seek reelection. The race has grown surprisingly competitive in a state that's shifted to the right in recent years, as affordability issues and the Trump tariff policies weigh on Iowans.
Maine

GOP Sen. Susan Collins is defending her seat against Troy Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner bowed out of the race in July following a sexual assault allegation. Collins has survived challenges in previous reelection fights, but Democrats are optimistic about their chances in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024 by almost 7 points.
Michigan

Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are vying for an open seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided to retire from Congress. El-Sayed is a progressive former Michigan health official who defeated a more moderate opponent in a divisive Democratic primary, while Rogers is seeking the seat after losing a bid to Sen. Elissa Slotkin last cycle.
Ohio

GOP Sen. Jon Husted is defending his seat against a comeback bid by former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in Ohio's other Senate seat last cycle. Democrats are hoping Brown's working-class brand will propel him to victory against Husted, the former lieutenant governor who was appointed to JD Vance's seat last year after Vance became vice president.
Texas

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and state Rep. James Talarico are competing in a closely watched contest in the Lone Star State. Democrats saw their chances of flipping the seat improve after Paxton defeated incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn, given Paxton's history of personal controversies and more conservative positions. But Republicans remain confident in their chances of holding onto the seat, though some concede that the race will be tough — and expensive.
Kansas

GOP Sen. Roger Marshall is aiming to prevent pastor Adam Hamilton from becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. Hamilton — a former Republican who leads the state's largest United Methodist church — has sought to capitalize on discontent around the cost of living, the Iran war and energy prices, which have hit Kansas farmers hard. Recent polls indicate a tight race, and national Republicans have poured millions into defending Marshall, who has cast Hamilton as a progressive in centrist's clothing.
Georgia

GOP Rep. Mike Collins is taking on Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia in a competitive race that was once expected to be the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans. But a messy Republican primary slowed the launch of Republicans' general election fight to unseat the first-term senator.
North Carolina

Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley are jockeying for a seat representing North Carolina in the Senate after GOP Sen. Thom Tillis announced he wouldn't seek reelection. Democrats see the seat in the Tar Heel State as a key prize, representing their best chance at flipping a seat this cycle.
New Hampshire

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and former GOP Sen. John Sununu are running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire to fill Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat upon her retirement. New Hampshire hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, but Republicans are hopeful about the prospects for Sununu, whose family has been dominant in Granite State politics.
House

All 435 House seats are up for election, with 218 as the threshold for the majority. The House is currently very narrowly divided, with 218 Republicans, plus an independent who caucuses with the GOP, and 214 Democrats. Two seats are vacant.
These are the 42 House races to watch:
Arizona's 1st Congressional District

Republican Jay Feely and Democrat Amish Shah are vying to replace eight-term GOP Rep. David Schweikert, who ran unsuccessfully for governor. Feely, an NFL veteran and former analyst for CBS Sports, initially ran in another district, but he switched at the urging of President Trump. Shah failed to unseat Schweikert in 2024.
Arizona's 6th Congressional District

Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani is up against Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza in the district that stretches from the Tucson-area suburbs down to the southeastern corner of the state along the U.S.-Mexico border.
California's 13th Congressional District

The seat held by Democratic Rep. Adam Gray is one of the House Republicans' campaign arm's top targets. Gray flipped the seat in 2024, narrowly winning by fewer than 200 votes. In 2022, he lost by fewer than 600 votes. In June's nonpartisan primary, he had a significant advantage over Republican Kevin Lincoln, a Marine veteran.
California's 22nd Congressional District

GOP Rep. David Valadao is one of two remaining House Republicans in Congress who voted to impeach President Trump in 2021 over the Capitol riot. He is the last one running for reelection, since Washington Rep. Dan Newhouse is retiring. Valadao is running against Democrat Randy Villegas in the newly redrawn district.
California's 45th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Derek Tran's district was redrawn as part of Gov. Gavin Newsom's redistricting push, making his new district one that Vice President Kamala Harris won by only 4 points. The House Republicans' campaign arm is backing former Cerritos Mayor Chuong Vo in its effort to target the Orange County-area district.
California's 48th Congressional District
Republican Jim Desmond and Democrat Marni Von Wilpert are on the ballot to replace outgoing GOP Rep. Darrell Issa in a newly redrawn Southern California district.
Colorado's 8th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Gabe Evans, who flipped a seat held by a Democrat in 2025, is running for reelection against Democrat Manny Rutinel, a progressive state representative. The district, which is north of Denver, has a sizable Latino population.
Florida's 14th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor's Tampa-area district has been redrawn to be more friendly to Republican, but it is still rated as Lean Democratic. Former state Rep. Mike Beltran won the crowded GOP primary to take on Castor in the fall.
Florida's 22nd Congressional District

After this district was gerrymandered to be more GOP-friendly, its congresswoman, Democrat Lois Frankel, opted instead to run in the 23rd District. Democrat Pia Dandiya won the August primary, and Republican Casey Askar prevailed in the crowded GOP primary. Both parties' campaign arms are targeting the district, which includes Palm Beach County.
Florida's 25th Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is running for reelection here, though the Boca Raton-area district's boundaries were altered to be more favorable to Republicans. Moskowitz faces former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer on the ballot.
Iowa's 1st Congressional District
Democrat Christina Bohannan is trying for a third time to unseat Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks. Miller-Meeks has won several close races since 2020.
Iowa's 2nd Congressional District
Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James are on the ballot to replace GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate.
Iowa's 3rd Congressional District
GOP Rep. Zach Nunn is defending his seat against Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott. Nunn, who has represented the Des Moines-area district since 2023, won reelection in 2024 by less than 4 points.
Michigan's 4th Congressional District
Longtime GOP Rep. Bill Huizenga is trying to fend off a challenge from Democrat Sean McCann, a state senator.
Michigan's 7th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Tom Barrett, who was first elected in 2024, is one of a handful of Republicans who have supported Democratic-led war powers resolutions to rein in President Trump on Iran. He's facing Democrat William Lawrence, who cofounded the Sunrise Movement and is a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
Michigan's 8th Congressional District

After suspending his campaign, Thomas Smith defeated a Trump-backed candidate to win the GOP primary and take on Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. Though the district elected McDonald Rivet in 2024, it also voted for President Trump.
Michigan's 10th Congressional District
Republican Michael Bouchard and Democrat Christina Hines are competing for the open seat, which is currently held by GOP Rep. John James, who is running for Michigan governor.
Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District

Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell are hoping to replace retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon in the Omaha-area district. Though the seat has been in GOP hands for all but two years in the last three decades, the district has voted for a Democrat in three of the last five presidential elections.
Nevada's 3rd Congressional District
Video game music composer Marty O'Donnell is hoping to unseat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee in the 3rd District, which touches parts of Las Vegas.
New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas opted to run for Senate this year, leaving the swingy seat open. Pappas has held the seat since 2017, but before that, it flipped five times between Republican and Democrats. Democrat Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo.
New Jersey's 7th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. is defending his seat against Democrat Rebecca Bennett, after his lengthy absence from Congress earlier this year. Upon his return to work in June, he disclosed he had been diagnosed with depression and was hospitalized for treatment.
New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District

Marine veteran Greg Cunningham is challenging Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez in the district, which spans the southern half of the state and includes part of Albuquerque. Vasquez was elected to the House in 2022, flipping the seat.
New York's 3rd Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi is defending his seat against former New York state Rep. Mike LePetri in the Long Island district. The longtime Democratic district flipped Republican in 2022, but after former Rep. George Santos was expelled from Congress, Suozzi won the special election for the seat. He was reelected in 2024, though Mr. Trump won the district.
New York's 4th Congressional District

In 2024, Democratic Rep. Laura Gillen defeated the Republican incumbent, Rep. Anthony D'Esposito, after he beat her in the race for the open Long Island seat in 2022. She'll face local tax receiver and GOP candidate Jeanine Driscoll.
New York's 17th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Mike Lawler has held the lower Hudson Valley seat since 2023, casting himself as a moderate who can work across the aisle. Democrat Cait Conley, a national security expert and Army combat veteran, moved to the district shortly before announcing her candidacy, though she grew up in the region. Harris narrowly won the district against Mr. Trump in 2024.
New York's 19th Congressional District
Democratic Rep. Josh Riley is trying for a second term in a district that has been competitive. GOP state Sen. Peter Oberacker is his opponent.
North Carolina's 1st Congressional District

The race is a rematch between Republican Laurie Buckhout and Democratic Rep. Don Davis. Davis is facing a tough reelection bid in a district that has leaned further to the right after several rounds of gerrymandering by state Republicans.
North Carolina's 11th Congressional District

GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his reelection bid after a House Ethics Committee investigation concluded he engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" toward two young women who worked for him. Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkom replaced Edwards on the ballot and will face Democrat Jamie Ager.
Ohio's 1st Congressional District

With Ohio's new court-approved congressional map, Republicans are targeting the 1st District, represented by Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman since 2023. Air Force veteran and former CIA case officer Eric Conroy won the crowded GOP primary with Mr. Trump's backing. Although Mr. Trump won the new district under its new boundaries, CBS News rates the district as Lean Democratic.
Ohio's 9th Congressional District

Voters have another chance to pick between longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur and Republican Derek Merrin. Merrin tried to unseat Kaptur in 2024, but lost by about 2,400 votes — just above the threshold needed to trigger an automatic recount. The Northwest Ohio district was redrawn in October 2025, creating a more Republican-leaning seat.
Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District

Democrat Bob Harvie is taking on GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who has been one of a few House Republicans to vote to limit President Trump's ability to further strike Iran. Fitzpatrick won reelection in 2024 by nearly 13 points.
Pennsylvania's 7th Congressional District
GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie flipped the district in 2024, beating the Democratic incumbent by 1 percentage point. This year, he faces retired firefighter Bob Brooks.
Pennsylvania's 8th Congressional District
Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan is running against Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. In 2024, Bresnahan defeated incumbent Democratic Rep. Matt Cartwright by less than 2 points.
Pennsylvania's 10th Congressional District

The race is a rematch between former TV news anchor Janelle Stelson and Republican Rep. Scott Perry. Stelson narrowly lost to Perry in 2024 by about 5,000 votes in the district that covers Harrisburg, York and the surrounding areas.
Texas' 15th Congressional District

Tejano musician Bobby Pulido is trying to unseat GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the Hispanic-majority district. De La Cruz flipped the seat in 2022 and President Trump won it by nearly 20 points in 2024, but Latino voters have shown a swing to the left since then.
Texas' 28th Congressional District

After Texas redrew its congressional districts, 11-term incumbent Democrat Henry Cuellar's district has become more friendly to Republicans. The GOP has long targeted Cuellar and considers the district a priority, but Cuellar has proven resilient. He also faced federal charges of bribery and money laundering, but Mr. Trump pardoned him last Decembercorruptionto have strength. Cuellar faces Republican Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina in November.
Texas' 34th Congressional District

Vicente Gonzalez prevailedsurvived in his 2024 race. Redistricting has made the district slightly more GOP-friendly, making it a top target for Republicansof House Republicans' campaign arm. Republican Mayra Flores is challenginggoing up against Gonzalez in the general election for a third time.

Casar opted to run in the new 37th District, leaving the 35th District open. Democrat Johnny Garcia and Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz, won their crowded primaries and are competing for the seatnow will face off on the ballot.
Virginia's 1st Congressional District

GOP Rep. Rob Wittman is hoping to extend Republicans' control of the seat for another two years. Republicans have held the seat since 1977. Wittman's Democratic rival is Henrico County's top prosecutor, Shannon Taylor.
Virginia's 2nd Congressional District

GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans is defending her seat against former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria, who represented the district for two terms before losing to Kiggans in 2022 after redistricting made the area more favorable to Republicans.
Washington's 3rd Congressional District

Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez twice defeated far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Trump's counterterrorism chief before he resigned in protest over the Iran war. This year she's defending her seat against John Braun, who has served in various leadership roles since his election to the state Senate in 2012. Mr. Trump won the district in 2024.
Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District

The race is a rematch between Democrat Rebecca Cooke and the Republican incumbent, Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who is running for his third term. Cooke, who owned a store that closed after the pandemic, lost to Van Orden in 2024 by less than 3 points. She has been balancing campaigning with waitressing, her website says.

title: Hearing over effort to deport Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Liberia abruptly canceled
summary: A hearing before a federal judge over whether Kilmar Abrego Garcia can be deported to Liberia was abruptly canceled on Tuesday.
story: Greenbelt, Maryland — A hearing before a federal judge over whether Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran man wrongfully deported by the Trump administration last year, can be sent to Liberia was abruptly canceled on Tuesday, leaving the matter unresolved for now.
Abrego Garcia's legal team was set to ask a federal judge to block his deportation to the West African country, where the administration has attempted to send him in his ongoing legal saga.

But the hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis in federal court in Maryland was delayed for 15 minutes before a court official informed the public that it was canceled. The courtroom was emptied shortly afterwards.
Abrego Garcia's attorney Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg told reporters the hearing was "unable to go forward" but did not comment on why. Justice Department attorneys also did not comment.

Abrego Garcia, who had been living in Maryland with his family, was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite a judge's 2019 order that blocked his deportation to the country on the grounds that he could be harmed by local gangs. The Trump administration had said Abrego Garcia was a member of the gang MS-13, which he has denied.
He was initially held at the Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT and was eventually returned to the U.S. in June 2025 to face criminal human smuggling charges.

In March, the Trump administration said that it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia, and asked Xinis to dissolve her order that is currently blocking that, or any other removal of Abrego Garcia, from happening.

In court filings, the Trump administration said that Liberia's government was willing to accept Abrego Garcia and that Immigration and Customs Enforcement could arrange a charter plane to send him to the West African country in a matter of days.

Liberia is among the countries that have agreed to accept non-native immigrants from the U.S., and the Trump administration began sending deportees from Latin America there in August. CBS News traveled to Liberia last month and interviewed a number of them. They described being in limbo and feeling stateless. They are unable to return to the U.S., where many have spouses and children, and said they are scared of being persecuted if they go back to their homelands.

Abrego Garcia has said he is willing to go to Costa Rica and designated the country as his preferred country of removal, and Costa Rica has indicated it would provide him refugee status or residency. But at a hearing last year, a Justice Department lawyer said there had not been discussions about deporting him there.

Tuesday's hearing would have been the first since a federal judge in Tennessee tossed out the criminal indictment charging Abrego Garcia with the alleged crimes, finding that the Justice Department's prosecution of him was vindictive. The government appealed that order in August.

In court filings ahead of the scheduled hearing, Abrego Garcia's lawyers said that the Trump administration is "trying to abuse its immigration powers to punish" him because their client had the "audacity" to challenge his removal to El Salvador.

"Just as the Government unlawfully wielded its criminal powers against Abrego Garcia, so it seeks to unlawfully exploit its immigration powers against him," they wrote in a motion for relief in May. "The record leaves no mystery about what is going on. If the Government truly wanted to remove Abrego Garcia from the United States, it would have sent him to Costa Rica in August 2025 when he designated it [as his country of removal]."
The Trump administration has also attempted to re-deport Abrego Garcia to the African nations of Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana, but none of the countries agreed to accept him.
The Justice Department said in court filings that Xinis should deny Abrego Garcia's motions because "his claims fail as a matter of law."
Abrego Garcia has remained free from ICE custody as his case has proceeded.

title: Olympian accused of damaging Reflecting Pool seeks probe of potential misconduct
summary: David Hearn is asking the Justice and Interior Dept. inspectors general to investigate his arrest and the dismissal of the case against him.
story: Attorneys for Olympic canoeist David Hearn asked the internal watchdogs at the Justice and Interior departments on Tuesday to investigate the circumstances surrounding his arrest, indictment and the dismissal of the case, according to a letter seen by CBS News.

Hearn's case garnered national attention, after he was falsely accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and subsequently indicted on a charge of felony destruction of government property.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, later moved to dismiss the case after she said new information had come to light showing the damage had been caused by a contractor's "botched installation," not vandalism.

"Because of the actions of various DOJ and DOI employees, Mr. Hearn was deprived of his liberty, indicted for a crime he did not commit, threatened with incarceration of up to 10 years, and endured the defaming of his name and reputation by high-ranking government officials," Hearn's attorneys wrote in the letter to DOJ Inspector General Don Berthiaume and DOI Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz.
Those officials, they pointed out, included Pirro, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and President Trump.

"The DOJ OIG and the DOI OIG must conduct detailed and comprehensive investigations to determine what happened inside their agencies that led to the shocking and indefensible treatment of Mr. Hearn," they wrote. "Anything less than a full and fair review would be a betrayal of your mission and perpetuate the outrageous mistreatment of Mr. Hearn."

Hearn was initially detained in jail for five hours on June 19, after he stopped by the Reflecting Pool during a bike ride. He put his hand into the water and touched a piece of the liner that had already come loose before he was asked by a member of the National Park Police to remove his hand from the water.

His lawyers said that during his five-hour detention, he was never read his Miranda rights or permitted to make a phone call, and that he only learned he was initially facing misdemeanor charges when he found two citations stuffed into a brown paper bag with his other belongings shortly after his release from custody.
A grand jury in the D.C. Superior Court later indicted him on the felony count on July 2.

Despite a request from Hearn's attorneys to preserve the physical evidence in the case, his lawyers said the government fenced off the area around the Reflecting Pool in question and undertook repairs to the section of the liner that was at the heart of the indictment.

By the end of July, Pirro moved to dismiss the case altogether, alleging that the Interior Department had delayed producing materials to prosecutors that undermined the evidentiary basis for the case.

"The record reflects an indictment obtained through unusual haste and a prosecution shaped from the outset by political pressure and built on an inadequate investigation," Hearn's lawyers wrote in the letter to the inspectors general.

Pirro was later spotted toting a large box into the White House that sources later confirmed to CBS News contained evidence from the case that she presented to Mr. Trump, after he lashed out at her for dismissing the case against Hearn.

The White House has since held meetings with prosecutors to explore whether other charges could be brought. But a Superior Court Judge foreclosed that possibility on Oct. 1, after he ruled that the case had to be dismissed with prejudice — meaning it cannot be brought again.

"Should the Court dismiss this case in a fashion that allows the government to reinitiate prosecution in the future, the Court would be exposing him to the risk that, due to pressure from the President Of the United States apparently motivated at least in part by Mr. Hearn's political views, he would again be charged with a crime that prosecutors have determined he did not commit," the judge wrote in the opinion dismissing the case.

The letter alleges that prosecutors had exculpatory evidence in hand before they sought an indictment against Hearn. It also alleges that Pirro improperly approached one of the defense's expert witnesses who was inspecting the Reflecting Pool and peppered the expert with questions.

"Defense counsel was given no notice that the encounter would take place and was not present for it, and the government has never produced any report, note, or record of the exchange," Hearn's attorneys wrote.

They continued, "A U.S. Attorney who personally interrogates a represented defendant's testifying expert, in the field, surrounded by her own staff and without notice to counsel, is not gathering evidence—she is testing how the defense intends to prove its case."

They also accused Pirro of running afoul of the rules of professional conduct for attorneys when she spoke publicly about the case during a press conference, and questioned whether the sole grand jury witness in the case had been recalled in order to "manufacture" a damages estimate to help support the felony charge.
Hearn's lawyers also complained that Pirro's statements announcing the indictment "extended well beyond the bare fact of the charge."

"[S]he previewed anticipated witness testimony, vouched for the credibility of government witnesses, opined directly on Mr. Hearn's guilt, and characterized the alleged conduct as 'anarchy' and 'criminal behavior' — conduct implicating the trial-publicity and prosecutorial-conduct constraints of D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct," Hearn's attorneys wrote.
A Justice Department spokesperson said, "The Office of the Inspector General operates independently and makes its own decisions about what to review."

title: Trump says he'll start paying for ads after pushback over taxpayer funding
summary: President Trump says he'll start paying for the pro-Trump ads that have blanketed the airwaves in recent weeks, using money from his super PAC instead of taxpayer dollars.
story: Washington — President Trump said Monday he will start paying for the pro-Trump ads that have blanketed the airwaves in recent weeks with money raised by his super PAC, after his administration drew intense pushback for using public funds on the ads.

"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," the president wrote on Truth Social. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."

A White House official said Tuesday morning that the president's post was not referring to reimbursing the federal government for ads that have already been purchased. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that "the ads were really good" when asked about the change and whether he would reimburse the government.
"They were promotion for the country," Mr. Trump said. "Done by many presidents before. So we'll decide."

Emblazoned with the message "Paid for by the U.S. Government," the ads began popping up late last month on national cable and broadcast networks, including CBS, as the November midterm elections approach.

Several variations have aired, including one that features a recording of Mr. Trump saying, "We will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America," as photos of the president flash across the screen. Another recounts the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
CBS News reported last month that there are multiple versions of the ads. The U.S. government produced the content and paid for the airtime through an ad agency.

The Department of Homeland Security awarded LMD Agency $20 million for a "National Media Campaign" starting on Sept. 20, contracting records show. A day earlier, the White House Office of Management and Budget granted DHS's Customs and Border Protection $20 million for "OBBB Commemorative Events," according to a nongovernment database. The source of the funds was first reported by The Washington Sun.
The White House has defended the ads, calling them public service announcements and denying that they constitute campaign advertisements.
A White House official said last month the PSAs "are clearly not political," and noted: "The President is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action."
Asked about the anti-communism ad, a spokesperson for the White House said: "The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country."

The advertising campaign has drawn bipartisan criticism. Democrats have argued the ads could violate federal laws that bar the use of government funds for "propaganda" purposes and limit political activity by executive branch employees.

"This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars," a group of Senate Democrats said in a letter last month.
A handful of Republicans have also voiced criticism.

"I don't think any public official, including President Trump or [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said on "Face the Nation."

By using his own super PAC to pay for the ads, Mr. Trump is tapping a nine-figure war chest that many Republican candidates hope will be spent in battleground states ahead of the midterms — despite a late start in this election cycle.

Since last month, the group has reported tens of millions of dollars in spending on the Texas Senate contest, where Trump-allied Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton is in a tight race against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico.

The group had more than $400 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Mr. Trump said last month he is "going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try and help us."

title: ABC asks judge to block FCC early license review
summary: An ABC lawyer argued the FCC was effectively forcing the broadcast company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about its license renewals.
story: An attorney for Disney's ABC asked a federal judge on Tuesday to block the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of the network's broadcast licenses, saying the regulatory proceeding was initiated to retaliate against ABC over content that offended the Trump administration.

During a roughly two-hour hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., ABC argued that comments from President Trump and FCC Chair Brendan Carr laid bare the true reasons behind why the regulatory agency took the unprecedented step in April of ordering eight television stations owned by ABC and its parent company to submit renewal applications for their broadcast licenses years ahead of schedule.
Those licenses were originally scheduled for renewal between 2028 and 2031.
"They are retaliating with their government power to stop ABC from exercising their protected First Amendment speech," said Beth Wilkinson, an attorney for the company.

Wilkinson at one point used the French Revolution to illustrate the FCC's actions, arguing the agency was effectively forcing the broadcast company to sit with its "head on a guillotine" while it awaits a decision about the licenses.

As the process plays out, she said, the regulatory action is having an immediate chilling effect on how ABC makes editorial decisions. Some of those decisions could in turn lead the FCC to "give us the corporate death penalty and take away our licenses," she said.

In her remarks, she highlighted a speech that Mr. Trump made at the White House in July, in which he chastised ABC and NBC for not broadcasting the speech and called for their licenses to be revoked. Those remarks, she said, represented a "direct threat" to her client.
"People may not like some of ABC's coverage and the president is entitled to it, but the public has the right to be exposed to different speech and viewpoints," she said.

The Justice Department, which is defending the FCC, has argued that the agency's decision in April to order an early license review was triggered by Disney's failure to adequately respond to an ongoing investigation into the company's diversity, equity and inclusion practices.

ABC "refused to adequately respond" to the FCC's anti-discrimination probe, said Dimitar Georgiev-Remme, one of the Justice Department's attorneys representing the FCC in the case. "The commission decided to look for information that it needed by calling for early renewal of plaintiffs' broadcast license."
Tuesday's legal arguments centered primarily on whether Disney and ABC have legal authority to challenge the FCC's early license renewal process in the district court.

The Justice Department argues that the regulatory process that governs license renewals would require a company to appeal an FCC order to the full commission. After that, any adverse decision can only be heard by a federal appellate court — and not a U.S. district court.

ABC, however, alleges that the type of retaliatory conduct it is facing in this case falls outside the scope of the regulatory appeals process prescribed by Congress, and this is the only way the company can seek relief to address the immediate harm it is facing.

In one such example of harm, Wilkinson said the network has changed the ways in which it covers political topics, noting that the talk show "The View" has changed how it selects the clips it uses in the show.

Comedian Jimmy Kimmel, a longstanding critic of Trump, also separately posted his interview with Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube rather than airing it with the network, she added.
Wilkinson said that even if the company had sought to appeal the April decision to initiate an early license renewal, the commission has the power to sit on the matter indefinitely.
She also noted that if the FCC ultimately decides to renew the licenses at the end of the process, ABC will have no effective legal remedy to address the harm it has suffered.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan, a Biden appointee, at times appeared skeptical at the government's claim that the FCC initiated the early license renewal process in order to get more information for its anti-discrimination investigation.

When she asked the Justice Department what other llegal tools it has at its disposal to compel ABC to provide the requested data, Georgiev-Remme could not provide an immediate answer, prompting the judge to ask the government to file a brief addressing her question by Oct. 9.

title: Ex-CIA official found with $40 million in gold bars admits to sprawling scheme
summary: A former CIA official admitted to inventing fake classified programs to divert nearly $200 million in government money that was used to buy Florida mansions and gold bars.
story: Washington — A former CIA official who was found with $40 million in gold bars in his home in May pleaded guilty on Tuesday, admitting he invented fake classified programs to divert nearly $200 million in government money that he used to buy Florida mansions and gold.
David Rush entered a guilty plea on a single count of wire fraud during a hearing in federal court in Virginia.
As part of his plea agreement, Rush agreed to forfeit at least $194 million, including 298 gold bars, two BMWs, 35 luxury watches and four luxury homes in Florida. He faces up to 20 years in prison.

In a filing known as a criminal information detailing the allegations Rush admitted to, prosecutors said he invented a fake classified program to steer $145 million in government funds through a front company, using the money to purchase the homes in Florida that he intended to resell for profit. Separately, he "fabricated a separate purported sensitive government activity to justify the acquisition of gold bars," prosecutors said.

"Although the real estate and gold acquisitions involved different transactions and intermediaries, they were executions of the same overarching scheme — RUSH created false classified authorities, directed and approved the associated expenditures, caused contractors and subcontractors to carry out the transactions, and thereafter exercised possession or control over the acquired assets," the filing said.

Prosecutors said Rush had access to "highly sensitive and classified government programs," although the filing does not name the CIA as his former employer. The spy agency and FBI said previously that the investigation began when the CIA referred the matter to the bureau. In the affidavit supporting the original criminal complaint against him, he was described as a "former Senior Executive Service level employee" at a government agency in eastern Virginia.

The document said Rush caused an unidentified contractor known as Company 1 to transfer about $145 million to a holding company set up at his direction. He then instructed employees at that company and a subcontractor to route that money to a holding company that he controlled, and used the funds to purchase four properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida.

Rush was arrested in May. FBI agents found the gold bars, $2 million in cash and luxury watches when executing a search warrant at his home. Prosecutors said Tuesday that the holding company had about $38.6 million left in its account.

The gold bars were purchased after Rush told the unnamed contractors "that he was working on a Top-Secret project in which he had to deliver high-value commodities to unnamed individuals," the information said. One of the contractors wired $45 million to the holding company in January, a transaction that forms the basis of the wire fraud charge.

Rush was originally charged with one count of stealing public money, with investigators saying he had provided false information about his education and military service on his government application, and fraudulently took military leave after his service ended.
In June, a federal judge ordered Rush to remain in custody as the case proceeded, determining that he posed a severe flight risk.

At his detention hearing, government lawyers called Rush a "master manipulator" who lied to his neighbors about being a pilot, lied to his co-workers and leveraged his "access to seniority." A Justice Department lawyer said Rush "cannot be trusted" and is "fully willing and able to skirt the rules."

Callie  Teitelbaum
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Conservative backlash after campaign ad shows lazy welfare recipient as White
summary: A campaign video from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders that portrays a welfare recipient as White has sparked a backlash from some conservatives.
story: Little Rock, Ark. — A new video from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders was standard issue Republican messaging for promoting her state's stricter rules for people on Medicaid. No more could able-bodied people lounge around while receiving taxpayer-funded healthcare, she said — they needed to work.

But the decision to portray an unemployed moocher as a young, White, cheeseball-chomping gamer named Brad upset some conservative commentators last week. Five decades after Ronald Reagan popularized the "welfare queen" trope about people living luxuriously while not working, they wanted to know why the video wasn't featuring a Black woman instead.

"Republicans don't have the balls to do this ad with 'Shaniqua' as the villain," posted Matt Walsh, a conservative writer. "Even though that would actually be an accurate portrayal of the problem at hand."

Sean Davis, co-founder of the Federalist website, wrote that "our government has systematically discriminated against White men for decades now, and yet now has the audacity to dishonestly mock young White men as welfare queens."

Never mind that the video was about Medicaid and not welfare, or that most Medicaid recipients in Arkansas are White. The outrage was a reminder of how old tropes are "chronically accessible" images in some voters' minds, said Ange-Marie Hancock, author of "The Politics of Disgust and the Public Identity of the 'Welfare Queen.'"

She thinks the Arkansas video was supposed to appeal to older voters living with unemployed adult children. But conservatives could only focus on race, Hancock said, because the idea of a Black welfare abuser has worked for them for decades.
"The longer race and gendered history really points to ideas that African Americans are lazy, they don't do the right thing," she said.

The debate that streaked across social media was the latest example of how conservatives have recently wrestled with racist views. Last month, a Texas political candidate named Bo French posted a picture of nonWhite students cheering at a University of Texas football game, saying "the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined." Some Republicans denounced French's post, while it was embraced by those who fear the country's changing demographics.
Sanders, who is running for reelection this year, "stands by the ad," said Jordan Powell, her campaign manager.
"We should never confiscate money from hard-working Arkansans to give it away to those who simply choose not to work at all," Powell told The Associated Press in an emailed statement.
Misconceptions about assistance programs persist
The "welfare queen" trope is often used to advance restrictions on public assistance programs.

While unsuccessfully running for president in 1976, Reagan complained about a woman in Chicago who was using "80 names, 30 addresses, 12 Social Security cards" to game the system. The story was embellished, but Reagan worked to reshape public assistance programs after winning the White House in 1980.

Allison Butler, author of "The Judgment of Gender: How Women are Centered and Silenced in Pop Culture," said the debate perpetuated a powerful myth that women of color were siphoning government assistance.

"When you deconstructed that narrative and actually tried to find the source of it ... there was no woman of color who wouldn't get a job and had multiple televisions and a Mercedes-Benz," Butler said.

Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference, has condemned the Sanders ad for reducing low-income people to a stereotype where poverty is seen as a flaw. It ignores the complexities that make it harder for low-income people, regardless of race, to support themselves, he said.
"We shouldn't betray anyone because they are asking for help and they don't meet your standards," Jefferson said.
The numbers tell what for some is an unexpected story

Created in 1965 as a joint federal and state health insurance program, Medicaid offers free or low-cost medical coverage to people with limited income including the elderly, children, or adults with disabilities who cannot work. Nearly 66 million people were enrolled in Medicaid as of June, according to the Medicaid.gov website.
Over 38% of beneficiaries between the ages of 0-64 are White, according to 2024 data from research organization KFF. Nearly 19% are Black.

More work requirements for some Medicaid beneficiaries kicked in across the U.S. this year under President Trump's big 2025 tax cut and policy law. A handful of Republican-led states, including Arkansas, are going beyond what the law calls for to prevent fraud including demanding more documentation if someone is too medically frail to work.

In July, Sanders soft-launched mandating that healthy people ages 19 to 64 find work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours per month to stay in the Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me Medicaid program, or ARHOME.

Robert Coon, managing partner at Impact Management Group, a political consulting and public-opinion firm with an Arkansas office, said that welfare work requirement policy is generally favored in Arkansas.
But suggestions the person in the ad should be Black are "overtly racist" and "inaccurate," Coon said.
About 60% of ARHOME recipients are White and around 18% are Black, according to recent data from the state Department of Human Services.

Right-wing rhetoric about Black Americans and public assistance often ignores how generations of structural racism have produced economic disparities that contribute to their disproportionate participation in these programs.

Fewer Black people than White people overall use social service programs like Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamps. But at roughly 13% of the U.S. population, Black people make up the largest overrepresentation of any racial group. They are 18.5% and 25%, respectively, of Medicaid and SNAP recipients.
Those statistics reflect an extremely difficult road for poor Black communities looking to rise out of poverty and build generational wealth.

Arkansas Democratic congressional candidate Chris Jones, who is Black, grew up in a family relying on food stamps. A welfare recipient is not "looking for a way out of work," but "for a way forward," he told the AP in a statement.
The bigger question, Jones said, is not about race but "why so many people who are working hard still struggle to afford groceries, housing, healthcare and the basic necessities of life."

Sarah Huckabee Sanders

title: Latino Dems urge investment in Hinojosa campaign as Texas governor's race tightens
summary: Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a new poll showed Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
story: Latino Democratic leaders are renewing calls for the Democratic Governors Association to invest more heavily in Texas after a New York Times/Siena College poll showed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa narrowly leading Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

The poll released Saturday found Hinojosa ahead of Abbott by three points, a result within the poll's margin of error. It comes as Hinojosa continues to face a huge financial disadvantage against the three-term Republican governor.  Abbott's reelection campaign and his Republican allies are outspending her by roughly 10-to-1.

More than 70 Latino Democratic leaders from across the country sent a letter this week urging the DGA and its chair, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race. The New York Times first reported on the letter, which CBS News has confirmed.

Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential contender, has been constrained by the DGA's commitments to first protect incumbent Democratic governors seeking reelection, though some of those incumbents are currently in strong positions.
In a statement, Beshear called Hinojosa a "great candidate" and said the DGA is "currently investing by paying expenses and providing staff, with more to come."
"My goal as chair of the DGA this year is to win as many races as we can and that's exactly what we're doing by going on offense and expanding the map," Beshear said.

Julián Castro, who served as secretary of housing and urban development in the Obama administration, renewed the push Saturday following the release of the New York Times poll. Castro, the former mayor of San Antonio and a 2020 presidential contender, took to social media to call for the DGA and Beshear to support Hinojosa "in a real way."
"How much more evidence" of Hinojosa's "strength in Texas" will Beshear and the DGA "have to see before they support her in a real way?" Castro wrote. "She can win!"

The renewed pressure comes as Democrats increasingly see the Lone Star state as competitive in the closing weeks of the campaign, even as Hinojosa continues to face a substantial spending disadvantage — what some Republicans are describing as a "firewall" — in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024.

title: Trump sending ACA and Medicare checks, but will they offset costs?
summary: President Trump sent $500 checks to some Affordable Care Act enrollees, while 20 million Medicare recipients will soon get $90 checks. Will they make a difference?
story: President Trump is sending checks to millions of Medicare and Affordable Care Act enrollees, with the White House describing the efforts as helping to "lower costs" for seniors and families. But experts say the payments may do little to offset rapidly rising healthcare expenses.
On Friday, Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration this month will send checks of about $90 to more than 20 million Medicare participants in the program's Part B plans.

That announcement followed the White House's Sept. 10 statement that $500 checks would be sent to about 1 million people who enrolled in an ACA plan this year through federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The payments, described as refunds for overcharges, are for people who didn't receive ACA insurance subsidies.

"President Trump is delivering on his promises to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans," the White House said in an Oct. 2 statement about the Medicare checks.

While the payments will help defray some of the healthcare costs paid by senior citizens and ACA-enrolled households, the money may not go far enough, health policy experts said. Americans cite healthcare costs as one of their top financial concerns, with almost 30% saying they've skipped or postponed healthcare treatments in the last year because of costs, according to polling from nonprofit health policy research organization KFF.

"A plan to lower healthcare costs is welcome, but President Trump's proposal to provide a one-time $90 payment to some Medicare beneficiaries will likely go unnoticed by most seniors," Max Richtman, CEO of the nonpartisan National Committee to Preserve Social Security & Medicare, told CBS News.
The White House said Mr. Trump is taking action to lower healthcare costs for millions of Americans.

"President Trump is enabling Americans to take control of their health by putting money directly back in the hands of Medicare patients," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said in a statement to CBS News. "In addition to guaranteeing discounted prices on prescription drugs through his Most-Favored-Nation drug pricing agreements, distributing $500 Obamacare Refund checks and increasing price transparency across the board, President Trump is delivering on his promise to lower costs for American patients by putting them first and taking on the special interests that have used the status quo in Washington to raise healthcare costs for Americans."

Mr. Trump has also promised $5,000 "dividend" payments to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain electoral control of both the House and Senate after the November midterms. Some economists and other experts have raised doubts about the feasibility of the payments, as they would require Congress to authorize more than $1 trillion in spending and could reignite inflation.
The Trump administration began sending the ACA checks on Sept. 30, while the Medicare checks will be sent starting in early October.
Higher Medicare Part B premiums

Premiums for Medicare Part B, which covers medical services such as doctor visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings, rose by more than $200 annually in 2026, and are forecast to rise by another $79 next year, according to June projections in the Medicare trustees' latest annual report.

That means the $90 check could fall short of covering the increased costs that seniors are already paying this year alone for their Part B plans, according to Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF.

"Receiving a one-time payment of $90 under this new plan from the Trump administration could be helpful, but it may not stretch very far when people are staring down higher costs for gas, heating their homes this coming winter, putting food on the table, keeping up with their mortgage payments," she said.
Rising ACA costs

Meanwhile, the $500 ACA check isn't likely to cover rising costs for people who get their health insurance through the program's marketplaces, said Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF.
The average premium for enrollees rose by $780 this year, up 58% from 2025, according to a KFF analysis.

ACA plan costs have risen sharply in 2026, partly due to the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits, which Congress allowed to lapse in December. Those tax breaks had helped lower premium costs for millions of middle-class Americans.

"People this year are paying significantly more than they were paying last year for health insurance on the individual market," Cox told CBS News. "It's going to help some people, certainly — getting a $500 check is better than not getting a $500 check — but for most people it won't cover their full increased costs."

A more effective method to lower healthcare costs would be to restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, Brian Keyser and Natasha Murphy of the Center for American Progress, a liberal-leaning think tank that supports the ACA, wrote in a Sept. 17 blog post.
Millions left out
About 40 million Medicare Part B recipients don't qualify for the $90 payment, while about 18 million ACA enrollees won't get a $500 check, enrollment data for the programs shows.

The $90 checks will go to seniors enrolled in Part B under traditional Medicare who don't pay income-related premiums or receive premium assistance from Medicaid. Seniors who are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans are also excluded from the checks, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
The Medicare check is reminiscent of President Trump's proposal to send a $200 drug card to help seniors with out-of-pocket drug costs before the 2020 presidential election, Cubanski said.

While that plan never got off the ground, it was also timed just before an important election. The new Medicare payments, to be disbursed by direct deposit, are set to arrive only weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon and ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, on Saturday called the $90 checks an "attempt to bribe the American public." But experts said the payments may barely register for some seniors.

"There's a question whether many of these payments might go unnoticed," Cubanski added. "People with Medicare get lots of mail from insurance companies and others trying to market plans during the open enrollment season, so this letter might get caught up in all the other mail that people are receiving."

title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced former House speaker, dies at 84
summary: Former Speaker of the House Dennis Hastert represented Illinois for two decades in Congress and was later jailed on charges related to his concealment of hush money payments made to cover up sexual abuse.
story: Washington — Former Speaker of the House Dennis Hastert, who represented Illinois for two decades in Congress and was jailed for violating banking laws to conceal payments made to cover up sexual abuse, has died, a coroner in Illinois said. He was 84.

Both the longest-serving Republican House speaker and the highest-ranking elected U.S. official to serve a prison sentence, Hastert's stunning fall from grace came in 2016, when he was sentenced to 15 months in prison on charges related to his concealment of hush money payments made to cover up his sexual abuse of teenage boys during his time as a high school wrestling coach.
Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell confirmed Monday that Hastert died at his home over the weekend due to natural causes. No further details were given.

Born in 1942 in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert grew up in a farming community. He went on to graduate from Wheaton College, where he received a degree in economics, before earning a teaching degree from Northern Illinois University. Hastert married Jean Kahl in 1973. The couple had two sons.

Hastert worked as a teacher in Illinois for 16 years while coaching wrestling. In 1976, he was named Illinois Coach of the Year. Four decades later, he would admit to sexually abusing boys during his time as a coach.
Hastert then served in the Illinois legislature, before going on to be elected to represent Illinois' 14th district in the U.S. House in 1986.

Hastert served in Congress from 1987 to 2007. With the mentorship of House Minority Leader Robert. H Michel, Hastert's profile grew among the GOP ranks, and in 1995, he became chief deputy whip. When former House Speaker Newt Gingrich stepped down in 1998, Hastert became the conference's second choice for his successor, following Rep. Bob Livingston's decision to step aside amid a scandal over extra-marital affairs.

Known as the "accidental speaker," Hastert would go on to become the longest-serving Republican speaker in history. During his tenure, Hastert, who had been a vocal critic of the Clinton administration, worked closely with former President George W. Bush on his policy agenda.

Among Hastert's most enduring imprints on the chamber is the rule that bears his name, which informally requires that the House vote only on measures that have a majority of support from the majority party in the chamber. The rule, which has faced criticism for making Congress more partisan, has posed hurdles for Republican House leadership in recent years.
After House Republicans lost the majority in the 2006 midterm elections, Hastert opted to leave leadership, before resigning from Congress in 2007.

Hastert became a lobbyist and consultant after leaving office. In 2013, the FBI and IRS began investigating the former speaker surrounding suspicions that he was illegally structuring bank transactions. In 2015, Hastert was indicted for structuring bank transactions to evade reporting requirements and making false statements to the FBI.

Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to violating banking laws by making repeated large cash withdrawals, which were revealed to be going to one of his victims. During the hearing, Hastert admitted to sexually abusing boys during his time as their wrestling coach. At his sentencing, U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin called Hastert a "serial child molester," and sentenced him to 15 months in prison, a $250,000 fine and ordered him to participate in a sex offender program. Hastert was not charged with sex-related crimes, as the statutes of limitations had expired. He served 13 months in a federal prison before his release in 2017.
Zachary Farden, the U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, said after Hastert was sentenced that there are "no winners in any of this"
"Mr. Hastert's legend and legacy are gone, and in its place are a broken, humiliated man," Farden said. "That is how it should be."

title: Sen. Tillis worries about the "outsized influence" of the executive branch
summary: Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, retiring soon, says without checks on power, U.S. democracy is at risk. He discusses his fears for the future of U.S. democracy and his relationship with President Trump.
story: As Sen. Thom Tillis exits the Senate, he's blasting many of the advisers President Trump has surrounded himself with as "sycophants," and calling on his colleagues to stand up to executive power like the coequal branch of government they are.

The 66-year-old senior senator from North Carolina unloads on what he calls the "WTF moments" of the second Trump administration in a new book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." Having served in the Senate during the Barack Obama, Joe Biden and both Trump presidencies, Tillis said he's increasingly worried about how the nation's system of checks and balances is being tested by the outsized influence of the executive branch.
"We will have a sort of dictator king if we're not careful," he said.
Make the Senate great again?

Every recent White House has been eager to govern by executive order, something that's been especially true during the current Trump administration, Tillis said. Presidents, he said, fail to understand that Congress is a coequal branch that should be treated as a peer, and that Congress needs to act as such.

"I would say the same thing for Democratic-controlled Senate under Biden and Obama," he said. "We always make the mistake when our guy's in office of conveying power to the White House. And I've had a real problem with that because it almost always comes back to bite you."
He writes in his book of the risks of authoritarianism. Tillis said there's been "constant escalation" across four administrations of presidents ignoring Congress.

"I want checks and balances. I want all three branches to have their individual role and continue to check power as they have for 250 years," he said. "I think because we've been such a successful democracy for so long, it's hard for the American people to understand how quickly we can lose it all."
The Tillis tightrope act

Tillis was first elected to the Senate in the 2014 midterm elections, just before the rise of Mr. Trump and his Make America Great Again populist movement took over the Republican Party. He said he's the same kind of conservative now that he was back then: "pro-Second Amendment, pro-life, limited government, fiscal restraint."
"The only difference between me and a lotta people that call themselves true conservatives is I got a long list of things that were ratified and they don't," he said.

The senator is now exiting Washington after a series of fights with the White House. The breaking point, he says, came in June 2025, after Tillis announced he would vote against Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, arguing that it would push too many low-income North Carolinians off Medicaid.

Mr. Trump responded by calling Tillis "a talker and complainer, not a doer," and threatening to back a primary challenger against Tillis. The senator decided he would retire instead of fighting for his seat.

"I respect the president. I still feel like we have an odd relationship, where I've clearly made him angry," Tillis said recently. That was before details of his profanity-laced private texts with Trump about what prompted his retirement leaked, because Tillis included them as part of his upcoming book.
Tillis said he is not done fighting, recently calling for Trump to fire Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

It should be noted that Tillis voted to confirm all of Mr. Trump's Cabinet nominees, including Hegseth.  But he now calls  that vote at the start of the second Trump administration his "biggest regret."

While Tillis said he is glad "the president went in" to Iran, he thinks "they got so caught up after the immense success of the first strike that Hegseth probably didn't listen to his best military advice and say, 'Now we should probably move to a different posture.'"

It's not the first time Tillis has gone after a member of Trump's Cabinet. Last March at a Senate hearing, he leveled a blistering critique of Department of Homeland Security Advisor Kristi Noem, calling out, among other things, the way she handled the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. That went viral, Tillis ripped into Noem. "I was thinking about her calling people that were shot, potentially domestic terrorists," he said. "That's proven not to be true."
Two days later, the president fired her.
"I think Noem and Hegseth are probably the poster children for men and women who should never have the authority they've been granted," Tillis said.

It's one example of the tightrope that Tillis has walked in the second Trump administration: saying how much he wants the president to succeed, while heaping blame on his advisers and subordinates. Besides Noem and Hegseth, Tillis is also highly critical of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, for "not looking around corners for" Mr. Trump.

Tillis' balancing act in Washington also extends to the events of Jan. 6, 2021. The senator is still angry about the attack on the Capitol, and threat to the peaceful transfer of power, calling what happened that day "despicable." Still, Tillis elected not to convict Mr. Trump after he left office during his second impeachment trial, criticizing the process as rushed and politicized.
"Cheapening the impeachment process to prevent somebody from running in the future, I just don't buy it," he said.
An "electoral bloodbath" in the midterms
Asked if he fears a Jan. 6-like reaction if Trump-supported candidates lose their elections during the midterms, Tillis was somber.
"I think there's a risk. I really do," he said, adding, "It would be another unforced error if we do that."

Tillis predicts Republicans are about to suffer an "electoral bloodbath" in the upcoming midterm elections, with bread-and-butter affordability issues a main concern. Still, he said many of his colleagues are afraid to break with the White House.

In his book, Tillis writes that at least 30 Republican senators have expressed reservations about many of Mr. Trump's actions, but usually are only willing to speak up privately, fearing that if the president decides to target them, their days will be numbered.

"They don't want to bear the weight of the president. I get that. You're up for reelection? He'll target you in a primary. And so look, you know what all martyrs have in common? They're dead," Tillis said. "There were probably a few instances where if [you] kind of ripped the bandaid off early, then I think we'd have had a lot better midterm environment than we're confronted with now."

title: Extreme heat putting births in jeopardy, U.N. climate chief warns
summary: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the U.N. climate chief is warning.
story: Nadi, Fiji — Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the U.N. climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.
This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the front line of climate change in the Pacific.
They are a precursor to the larger U.N.-sponsored global climate summit, known as COP31, to be held in Turkey next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.
"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.
The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardizing homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
Fiji's climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, called for commitments from developing nations to a "just transition" with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most."
A U.N. report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion to $365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
"We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said.

Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter— faces accusations of hypocrisy: Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.
Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with her Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials.
"Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.
"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.
Refocusing on limiting global warming

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a threshhold that was breached in 2025 — and give more attention to the impact on oceans.
"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.
"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table,'" he said.

Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August U.N. report.  .Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, it said.
Regional leaders have pitched the pre-COP as a chance to bring the world to the Pacific, and they are keen to show the impact climate change is having on the region.
In Naidiri Village, a marine protected area an hour's drive south of Nadi, locals described efforts to combat coral bleaching and improve ocean health.
"Countries that don't cause climate change are being affected," Joseva Kunagado, 21, told AFP.

Manoa Duwai, who set up Naidiri Village's marine protected area more than a decade ago after realizing what the damage wrought by overfishing is, said they were experiencing climate change "every day."
"The sea level is rising, and a heat wave earlier this year," he said. "A message to the developed countries: Do remember, don't forget."
Delegates will also take a one-day trip on Tuesday to low-lying Tuvalu, which is already laying plans to relocate its population if it's consumed by the ocean.
Tuvalu is one of the world's least visited countries and the highest point in its capital, Funafuti, is just 6.6 feet above sea level.
