title: Trump temporarily expands use of red-dyed diesel. Will it lower costs?
summary: Experts say the new executive order will have a limited impact on farmers and truckers who rely on diesel.
story: President Trump's new executive order allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways is aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers grappling with diesel prices that remain near record highs. But experts say they are skeptical that the order could deliver sweeping savings.
"It might lead to savings for some, but there are a lot of details that will prevent this from having widespread relief," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News.

Mr. Trump announced the executive order on Tuesday during a midterm rally in Nebraska, saying the move will "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dye diesel for any reason."
Before the EO passed, farmers had to buy regular diesel for their trucks and on-road vehicles, which is subject to excise taxes, a White House official told CBS News in an email.
Now, they can use red-dyed diesel, which is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The EO comes as diesel prices remain high, although they've eased slightly after reaching a record high last month of $6.53 a gallon. High diesel prices are placing financial strains on the nation's transportation, construction and agricultural industries, which rely heavily on the fuel to move goods and power equipment.
On Tuesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.32, according to AAA, compared to $3.76 before the war in Iran started.
Read on to learn more about red-dyed diesel.
What is red-dyed diesel?
Red-dyed diesel is tax-free diesel intended for off-road vehicles, including farm and construction equipment.

The fuel is dyed red because it allows state law enforcement to easily spot it if drivers are using it on roads and highways in an effort to skirt taxes. Violators may face large fines or penalties, including tax evasion.

Mr. Trump's executive order temporarily removes the limits on red-dyed diesel, allowing all drivers to use it without incurring taxes or penalties. However, it doesn't entirely eliminate taxes on red-dyed diesel.

Instead, it defers the federal excise tax for the remainder of 2026 and directs the Treasury secretary to explore ways to eliminate the requirement to pay the taxes, according to the White House. That means drivers could potentially be on the hook for a payment down the road, experts said.
"Whether anyone who makes the switch to dyed diesel suddenly gets a tax bill is the most unanswered question I have," De Haan said in a post on X.
The White House official said drivers will be liable for the deferred tax only if the Internal Revenue Service, at the direction of the Secretary of the Treasury, takes action to enforce it.
Will the Trump administration's EO lead to cost savings?
According to a White House fact sheet on the executive order, drivers who rely on diesel could save more than $100 each time they fill up.
However, many states also have bans on using red-dyed diesel on roads and highways. The White House said it is working with states to encourage them to also waive the ban.

But if some states don't waive their bans, it could lead to a "convoluted patchwork" of enforcement, which may ultimately deter trucks that need to cross state lines from using red-dyed diesel, De Haan added.

"If one state is enforcing red-dyed diesel and a trucker crosses over with dyed diesel, that could spell trouble, and [lead to] enforcement issues," he said. "Most of the large end users that could stand to benefit from lower prices probably won't get much of the benefit behind this."
The impact on farmers will also be muted, given that they already get tax-free diesel in most states, De Haan noted.
"Most of them have thousands of liters that they've been buying at tax-free, at scheduled intervals, I should say, and so it's not really any huge advantage," he told CBS News.

The EO will allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel in personal vehicles, but it will yield only minimal savings, he added. "I don't think that any farmer is going to be jumping for joy at the prospect of saving, you know, 50 or 60 cents a gallon on their personal vehicle."
Fails to address the supply issue
Experts noted that the EO doesn't address the lack of diesel supply, the key issue keeping prices elevated.
"The U.S. has about 105 million barrels of diesel in  inventory," Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News in an email. "This move doesn't increase or decrease that level."
In theory, the EO should still put downward pressure on diesel prices; however, swings in the diesel market could blunt progress toward lower prices, Kloza added.
Lowering prices without increasing supply could also stimulate demand, which could have the unintended consequence of driving up costs, De Haan pointed out.
"Part of the reason why we have these high prices is because economics is telling us that there are imbalances," he said. "So to ignore them and go ahead with this risks exacerbating the issue."

title: Supreme Court wrestles with energy companies' bid to block major climate suit
summary: Eight of the nine justices heard nearly two hours of oral arguments in a case involving an effort by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, to hold energy companies accountable for the effects of global climate change.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday grappled with a complex dispute involving an effort by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, to hold energy companies accountable for the effects of global climate change.

Eight of the court's nine justices heard nearly two hours of oral arguments in the case Suncor Energy v. Commissioners of Boulder County. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from the case, the Supreme Court said last week.

No reason was given for Alito's decision to sit out the case. His financial disclosure for 2025 shows that he had individual holdings in two energy companies, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Alito did not report holding individual stocks in either Exxon Mobil or Suncor Energy, the two companies that Boulder filed its lawsuit against in 2018.

Alito's recusal leaves open the possibility that the Supreme Court deadlocks 4-4 in the case. That outcome would mean the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court would stand, allowing Boulder's case to proceed.

Boulder's dispute against Exxon and Suncor remains in its early stages. At issue before the Supreme Court is whether the lawsuit can proceed or is barred by federal law. The high court also asked lawyers for both sides to address whether it has jurisdiction to review the Colorado Supreme Court's decision.

In questions to both Kannon Shanmugam, who argued on behalf of Exxon and Suncor, and Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general, Justice Brett Kavanaugh repeatedly said that four of the Supreme Court's decisions dating back to 1972 make clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters of federal law.

"We don't have to reinvent the wheel, because we've said this multiple times and Congress, presumably when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this court's precedents establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal-law matter, unless Congress speaks otherwise," he said.

The Trump administration is backing Exxon, the nation's largest oil company, and Suncor, which operates two oil refineries in Colorado, in the case. Boulder's lawsuit, Harris said, "egregiously exceeds" constitutional limits of state authority.
"Interstate air pollution is an inherently federal area, and Congress hasn't authorized this suit in the Clean Air Act," she said.
But Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson stressed that the Supreme Court's review is "premature."
"It feels like we don't really know enough to be confident that the theories that you are proposing are actually applicable here," she told Harris.
Boulder's lawsuit against Suncor and Exxon

The lawsuit from the city and county of Boulder is one of dozens filed by states and local governments against energy companies in state courts that seek money damages for past and future harms that they allege are caused by the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which has led to global warming.

Boulder alleges in its suit that Exxon and Suncor's conduct has caused or contributed to climate change, which has in turn forced the city and county to confront extreme heat, larger and more frequent wildfires and damage to the ecosystem, among other issues.

The city and county raised several claims under state law and argued that the energy companies' production and allegedly deceptive marketing of fossil fuels has led to "unchecked" use of their products that has caused a rapid rise in the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

Exxon and Suncor attempted to move the case to federal court, but that effort was unsuccessful. The companies also asked the Boulder County District Court to dismiss the case on the grounds that federal law foreclosed the claims against them. When the state court denied that request, the companies asked the Colorado Supreme Court to step in.
The state's high court sided with the city and county of Boulder, and Suncor and Exxon appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

"It's taken a long time to get to this point, but it feels very positive that that effort that we started in this exact location eight years ago has gotten to the stage of going to the Supreme Court, and then hopefully the next step of having a full hearing in court," Boulder Mayor Aaron Brockett said after a rally in downtown Boulder on Monday.
"People care very much about climate change in Boulder. They recognize the existential threat that it provides to our society, and so people are very supportive of this lawsuit," Brockett added.
The Supreme Court's arguments

Shanmugam, who argued on behalf of Exxon and Suncor, told the justices during arguments that the Constitution and the Clean Air Act preclude claims that seek to address the harms caused by interstate greenhouse-gas emissions. He also warned that efforts like Boulder's to secure relief from the effects of air pollution undermine the government's control over foreign affairs.
Shanmugam called Boulder's lawsuit an "unprecedented effort" to use state law to regulate global conduct, which is not allowed under the nation's constitutional system.
"A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state," he said.

Shanmugam warned that if Boulder's lawsuit is allowed to go forward, 90,000 municipalities could file similar challenges and "have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers."
Chief Justice John Roberts, too, noted that if Boulder prevails before the Supreme Court, local governments in every state will file their own lawsuits similar to Boulder's.
"How would you think that will work out on the ground?" he asked Kevin Russell, who argued on behalf of Boulder.
Russell stressed that even if Boulder's case can move forward, more litigation over the specifics of the suit will follow.
But Roberts also said there are other instances where the Supreme Court has allowed state-court lawsuits involving issues with wide impacts to go ahead.

"There are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects from other states and all that, and yet we allow state courts in a particular state to bring litigation that affects that, whether it's a mass tort sort of thing or maybe complaints about operations of the internet," the chief justice said. "I guess I'm not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we've allowed them to proceed in state court."

Justice Elena Kagan, meanwhile, said the case against the energy companies appears similar to lawsuits brought against tobacco companies in the 1990s and pharmaceutical companies in response to the opioid epidemic.
"This is chapter three," she said, noting that state claims against those companies could proceed.
But Kavanaugh said later that "this court has consistently said that air and water pollution are different in our federal enclaves."

Lawyers for Boulder city and county are urging the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on the grounds that it does not have jurisdiction. If the justices opt not to, they say the Colorado Supreme Court decision should be upheld.

"Since the founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders, even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere," Russell told the justices.
He also argued that Congress "stands at the ready" to intervene and enact federal law that preempts "unreasonable state laws."

"This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change; it merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct," Russell wrote in a filing.
He also told the justices that Boulder did not sue for emissions, which are regulated by the Clean Air Act, but over allegedly deceptive marketing and production, which that law does not regulate.

"It is not an effort to reduce emissions," Russell said. "Under our deception theory, they can continue to produce as much fossil fuels as they like and contribute to as much air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, as the market will bear when consumers are properly informed about the consequences of that decision."
A decision from the Supreme Court is expected by summer of 2027.

Sarah  Horbacewicz
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Shock gloves bought by ICE cause intense pain, Army study says
summary: Participants in a military exercise felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to an Army study.
story: The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.

The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again," the study found.
"After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply," the authors wrote.
Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns

In contract paperwork released on a federal database in August, ICE called the gloves "distraction and de-escalation devices" that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance the gloves cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.

"ICE does not currently have an empty hand use of force device to provide to the field amid unprecedented levels of threats and violence against ICE officers and agents to help ensure they can de-escalate tense situations before they turn violent," the agency wrote in procurement documents.

But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or disabled people.

"The military assessment in ICE's own files shows that these gloves can cause 'intense pain' and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe," said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. "Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it."
ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.
Study found shock gloves triggered "immediate" compliance

The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.

The study found the devices "increased the efficiency" of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not "significantly change" the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.
"GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members," the study found. "Inmate compliance was immediate" compared to other methods, it added.

The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead "works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings" of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.
Senator says ICE hasn't responded to demand for details on gloves' use

ICE's contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.
The six-month deal includes the gloves, support equipment and services. The gloves themselves cost $2,495 apiece.

Compliant Technologies' instruction manual says users of the gloves should "always give the subject(s) a reasonable opportunity to comply before force is used." It suggests using them for up to 15 seconds, unless the subject becomes more violent or endangers people.

White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could "be awhile" before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said "officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics."

U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.

"Without ICE's responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received," she said.

The Department of Homeland Security has defended the purchase, accusing critics of trying to deny federal law enforcement officers safety equipment. In a statement to CBS News in August, a DHS spokesperson called the pushback from Democrats "despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers."

"ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards," the spokesperson said, adding that personnel are "highly trained in de-escalation tactics."

Joe  Walsh and 
                                                  
                                  Nicole  Sganga
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Details emerge in case of former Cornell student alleging rape by frat members
summary: A woman, identified only as Jane Doe, alleges she was gang-raped by seven fraternity members in 2024 and accuses Cornell University of failing to protect her.
story: New details are emerging in the case of a former Cornell University student who claims she was drugged and gang-raped for multiple hours inside a fraternity house in October 2024.

The woman — identified only as Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged incident — recently filed a civil lawsuit against seven then-Chi Phi fraternity members and the university, claiming they failed to protect her and prevent the alleged assault. While Cornell conducted an internal investigation, and expelled or suspended several of the men, no criminal charges were brought against the accused at the time.

The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office confirmed on Monday, Sept. 28, that it was reopening the criminal investigation amid pressure from the community. The DA said the woman's sworn statement from November 2024 was different from what she alleges in the civil lawsuit, while her attorney claims investigators never followed up on her allegations.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 1 signed an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor in the case. Hochul said James will "investigate the incident and, if warranted, prosecute any offenses arising from the investigation and present evidence to a grand jury."
Here is what we know about the case so far:
Claims against Cornell

In the lawsuit against the university and the then-fraternity members, the woman alleges she visited a friend at Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity house while she was already intoxicated, and alleges that two fraternity members pressured her into taking what they said was ketamine. She alleges they then sexually assaulted her.

According to the suit, on the night in question at around 1:42 a.m., one fraternity member sent a crude message to a Chi Phi Snapchat group chat suggesting that a woman upstairs was available for sex. The woman alleges more men entered the room and the assaults continued until 5:45 a.m.
The complaint says the woman filed a report with the university's police department three weeks after the alleged rapes.

"Once she was emotionally ready, she went to the University police and bravely shared what had occurred to her. She went to the police because she believed that she was the victim of a crime," her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement to CBS News.

"Other than her initial contact with Cornell Police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors," Giuffra said.

Cornell conducted an internal review of the allegations after she filed the report with campus police. Giuffra told CBS News New York that two of the fraternity members were expelled, while five others received lesser sanctions including suspensions, workshops and writing essays.
"Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact," Giuffra told CBS News New York, adding that the woman dropped out of the school after the alleged assault.
Cornell disputed the idea that some of the accused only had to write essays for punishment.
"None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," the university said.

Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff specified in a Sept. 29 meeting with the student government that two of the accused were expelled, two suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.

The lawsuit accuses Cornell and the other defendants of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law. She is seeking monetary damages, including compensatory and punitive damages. The lawsuit does not specify how much she is seeking.
Exclusive report on Jane Doe campus police interview transcript

According to a transcript of the alleged victim's interview with campus police, obtained by CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi from a source, Jane Doe distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later in the night.
She described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory, according to the transcript.
When asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The interview began on Nov. 14, 2024 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day.

The transcript was used as the basis for the alleged victim's written statement, and it shows the investigator read her account back to her word by word and gave her a chance to clarify or correct the record.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wanted her and another adviser to review the statement.
In the statement, obtained by CBS News, she detailed what she said happened the night of the alleged rape. She described being "pretty incapacitated" and things becoming a blur.
She recalled "multiple men" coming into the room at some point when she was naked.

"I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out. My thought was that if I passed out and these men have sex with me, then they could have been charged with rape at this point," she said in the statement.
Later, she described two people walking in and saying they were "shutting it down," which caused "the group of men" to scatter.

She then described sexual encounters. "I remember being totally disgusted at the situation, and I felt very tired and intoxicated," she said, adding, "I would say that it was the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life. I felt like I was unable to make any decisions because of how intoxicated I was."
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBS News on Sept. 29 that he was never provided the full transcripts of those initial interviews Jane Doe conducted with Cornell police.

He said the sworn statement submitted to his office in November 2024 made no mention of the statements that were made in the transcript obtained by CBS News New York — specifically Doe telling school investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
"I never saw it, never heard it until tonight," Van Houten said in the interview. "If it exists, I will get it. You can be sure of that."
He added, "If that kind of thing was omitted from a statement, if it is true, it needs to be fully investigated by someone outside of Cornell."

Cornell University initially said its police department provided the results of the school's investigation to the DA. However, in an FAQ published on its website regarding the allegations, the university said in an Oct. 1 update that it "shared the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."

Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, remarked to CBS News, "What more did (Van Houten) need to do a thorough investigation and prosecute? He had a woman who told an officer she was raped and a group chat inviting sexual assaults. The failure to do anything is shocking.

"Neither I nor Ms. Doe have any confidence in DA Houten's ability to handle this investigation and prosecution. He seems more interested in protecting his reputation as opposed to seeking justice as is his duty as the District Attorney."
Title IX investigation transcripts

CBS News New York obtained transcripts of Cornell's Title IX investigation, distributed to the parties in January 2025, from a source. The documents are part of the record but do not include the Title IX panel's hearing minutes, reasoning or final findings.

The records offer a closer look at how Jane Doe described what she says happened to her that night and in the days that followed, as well as how people around her remembered it. They include interviews with Doe, six of the seven men named in Doe's bombshell civil lawsuit, and 20 witnesses.

One roommate recalls Doe saying "Oh my goodness, isn't that crazy?" the morning after the alleged incident at Cornell's Chi Phi house in October 2024. The roommate said Doe was laughing as she recounted it, but seemed to be in shock. The roommate said Doe did not call it rape or assault that next morning.
A second roommate said Jane Doe did tell her "I wasn't comfortable."
About a week later, that second roommate said she heard Doe tell one of the men, "You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me."

In her Title IX interview in November, Doe said she didn't show "excitement and enthusiasm, which is kinda the basis of consent." She said she told the men she was tired and didn't want to continue, and that she was sometimes encouraged to take more substances.
The men, now accused of rape and assault, also gave their accounts.
One said he asked Jane Doe if he could take ketamine from her body. He said she agreed.

Another, Scott Kretzschmar, said he was in the room for "tops, five minutes," did not see her naked, and did not do drugs. Kretzschmar told a Title IX investigator he asked Doe if she was OK. He said her response was "I'm good" and that "she didn't seem inebriated at all."
The allegation against Kretzschmar is that he snorted ketamine from Doe's body, something his attorney Jeremy Saland denies.
Cornell said its Title IX process lasted months, included a hearing before a panel of trained faculty and staff, and resulted in sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions.

"After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days," Cornell's statement said. "The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence."
Cornell's response and internal investigation
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said on Sept. 30 that Cornell has agreed to bring in outside counsel for an independent investigation. "I want answers. And I want accountability," she wrote on X.
Cornell said on Oct. 6 that former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will oversee a broad review of the university's handling of sexual misconduct claims, including Jane Doe's allegations.
The fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."
The Ithaca Police Department told CBS News New York that the alleged incident was never reported to them.

Cornell said in a statement that Ithaca police were not involved initially because the "established protocol" when the school's police department believes a crime may have been committed is to share the investigation with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office.

"The Cornell University Police Department is a sworn law enforcement agency and performs the same functions as municipal police, but on Cornell property. This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction," the school said.
Former Cornell University police chief Anthony Bellamy, who is now deputy chief at the Ithaca Police Department, told CBS News he has no comment.
Van Houten told CBS News that the DA's office didn't have access to Cornell's Title IX records on the alleged incident, and that he's asking Jane Doe's attorney to provide those documents.
He also said "we don't have any indication" campus police at the time interviewed the seven then-fraternity brothers accused in the lawsuit.
Snapchat and text messages
CBS News New York exclusively obtained additional video of the fraternity's group Snapchat conversation from the night the woman alleges the incident occurred.
A message sent to the group at 1:42 a.m. suggested in crude language that a woman was available for sex.
"Shop still open?" one fraternity brother wrote later.
The response was "Yea."

Screenshots of a separate text exchange, also reported exclusively by CBS News New York, show what a source describes as messages sent two days later between Jane Doe and one of the defendants now accused in the lawsuit.

The man started by apologizing for "how things went down." He said his memory is "kinda fuzzy," and that he and another man feel bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand."
The woman in the text chain replied that her memory is "super clouded too," and said they had all been heavily intoxicated.

She also wrote, "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal." She said she liked being with him and another man. Later, she suggested they smoke together again, "but like leave out the extra 5 billion men and ketamine."
The woman's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, confirmed she exchanged texts with this defendant shortly after the alleged assault, but he could not confirm whether these were the specific texts.
Giuffra said she was in denial and traumatized shortly after the alleged assaults. He said she was intoxicated to the point of incapacity that night and was trying to find out what happened.
He said she felt like she should not take an aggressive tone with this defendant if she wanted answers.
N.Y. Attorney General Letitia James appointed as special prosecutor
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order naming New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case.

"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard," James said at a news conference Friday, Oct. 2. "That is the promise of our justice system. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law."

Hocul said in a statement that she asked James to take over the case because "[n]ewly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute," saying it had "undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the District Attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."
A Cornell spokesperson said the university supports the decision to assign the case to James' office.
The appointment comes less than a week after the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office said it would  reopen the criminal investigation — a decision Cornell also said it supported.

Before James' appointment, the DA, Matthew Van Houten, had told CBS News correspondent Lilia Luciano that he hoped they'd be able to bring the case to a grand jury "in the next 45 days," adding, "I want to move fast." He had said the grand jury could "consider the charges that were set out in the civil complaint, and they can consider other charges."

In a statement earlier, Van Houten said the allegations made in the civil lawsuit were different from the sworn statement made by Jane Doe in November 2024. He said her 2024 statement "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped" by multiple men.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten's statement said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."
He told CBS News, "I don't see how more could have been done at the time, given that foundation of the case being her statement."
Van Houten called the Snapchat message chain "disgusting, vulgar," but said it "had nothing to do with the issue of consent, which is the legal issue."
Cornell said the Cornell University Police Department provided a screenshot from Snapchat to the DA back in 2024, along with Jane Doe's sworn statement.

Van Houten told CBS News the officer who took Jane Doe's original statement was "an experienced investigator" who was "trained in trauma informed sexual assault cases," and "not just somebody who was manning the desk."

He had told CBS News: "We want to treat her with respect and with humanity and compassion and hear from her what's changed since November of 2024. We want to sit down with her and talk through what she knows now and what she has processed over that time so that we can put all of the evidence before the grand jury and let the grand jury decide."
Giuffra, the woman's attorney, said she was not contacted by investigators from the DA's office after she made her report to Cornell's university police.

"Interviewing a survivor is a challenging process that takes a lot of time and experience. It is never easy for a survivor to share details of an assault with a stranger. Trust must be developed and a lot of time spent learning the facts and engaging with the survivor," he said. "It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint."
Giuffra told CBS News they welcomed the reopening of the criminal investigation, saying it was "a step in the right direction, albeit a late one."
Defendants deny accusations
The lawsuit identifies one of the accused then-fraternity members as Scott Kretzchmar, who allegedly sent two responses in the Snapchat group.
His defense attorney, Jeremy Saland, acknowledged to CBS News that the messages were inappropriate but said they are not evidence of sexual assault.
"This is a situation where there was an ugly Snapchat — ugly, period. … But that doesn't make my client a rapist, and it certainly doesn't make anyone a sex offender," Saland said.

Saland said Kretzchmar briefly entered the room where the woman was, in response to the message "that many people have seen," and said he did not touch her "in any way, shape or form" and left in a matter of minutes.
"She was not incoherent but in fact was coherent and again left that room without touching her or having any physical interaction with her whatsoever," Saland said.
The attorney said the university found Kretzchmar was not responsible for anything that the woman alleges in her complaint.
As for the accusation of ketamine use, Saland said Kretzchmar took a hair follicle test that determined he had no ketamine in his system.
"We certainly would present evidence of the hair follicle test which demonstrably and scientifically shows that he did not ingest ketamine as alleged by the complainant," he said.
Saland said that while no one has contacted him about a renewed investigation, "we welcome the opportunity."

"We are available to present exonerating evidence. I just hope the right thing is eventually done, this case is closed, and my client can live his life and not be subject to this selfish, repugnant, vile claim by this woman about him," he added.

Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing Gillio Lopes, another then-fraternity member accused in the civil lawsuit, told CBS News New York that his client "unequivocally denies the allegations against him."

"Cornell previously investigated these allegations. The allegations now being made publicly differ from what was reported and investigated during that process," Miltenberg said. "These are serious accusations, but accusations are not proof. Mr. Lopes should be judged on the evidence, not prejudged based on allegations made in a lawsuit or repeated in the media. We will address these issues through the appropriate legal process."
CBS News has reached out to the other defendants named in the civil lawsuit.
Mahsa Saeidi, Lilia Luciano and Kinjal Patel contributed to this report.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed Dec. 3, email states
summary: Nidal Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
story: An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, 2026, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.
Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday that the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
CBS Texas has reached out to Fort Hood for comment and was directed to Army headquarters.

In addition to the 13 people Hasan killed on Nov. 5, 2009, 32 others were injured. Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.
The last military execution took place 65 years ago, when the Army executed Pvt. John Bennett by hanging after he was convicted of rape and the attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.
The last execution by firing squad happened during World War II, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was put to death in France for desertion.

Hasan, now 56, was an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shootings. He had served two decades in the Army. Witnesses described hearing Hasan shout "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down when police returned fire.
Since his conviction, Hasan has been on death row at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.
Why a firing squad?

According to Army regulation 190-55, military executions can only be approved by the president. A 2019 revision removed the term "lethal injection" from this regulation and left the method up to the secretary of the Army's designation. According to the guidelines, the method is recommended to the secretary by the provost marshal general.

According to this order, the prisoner is informed of the president's decision in person by the commandant, who is accompanied by a chaplain and, if available, a defense attorney. After the notification, the prisoner becomes a "condemned prisoner."
The victims

Family members of those who died were notified of the planned execution before the announcement was made. They, along with survivors, were asked if they wanted to attend. The group, bonded in tragedy, has been intertwined over the last 17 years. This is what many hope will be the final chapter in the tragedy.
Below are the names of those who died.
Lt. Col. Juanita Warman, 55
Maj. Libardo Eduardo Caraveo, 52
Capt. John P. Gaffaney, 56
Capt. Russell Seager, 51
Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow, 32
Sgt. Amy Krueger, 29

Pfc. Michael S. Pearson, 22
Pfc. Kham S. Xiong, 23
Pvt. Francheska Velez, 21 (and her unborn child)

title: California couple at center of surrogacy scandal arrested
summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who had at least 25 children via surrogates, were arrested at their home in Arcadia, California.
story: A California couple at the center of a surrogacy scandal was arrested on Tuesday. A law enforcement source confirmed the arrests to CBS News shortly before officials held a news conference to announce the latest developments.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang are being charged with multiple counts, including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said.
The couple drew national headlines last year after authorities raided their Arcadia mansion in July 2025 and took 21 kids, mostly surrogate-born, into state custody.

Tuesday morning, detectives from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the couple at their residence. They were then transferred to the Pasadena courthouse to be arraigned, Sheriff Robert Luna said. They both pleaded not guilty and are each being held on a $20 million bond.
A neighbor said Tuesday that helicopters and police could be seen at the couple's mansion and the entire block is taped off.
"What has been publicly filed in the complaint today is incredibly disturbing. It involves horrific punishment and beatings and child abuse," Hochman said at the news conference.
Officials said the investigation began in May 2025 when Zhang brought a 2-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury.

"She appeared to be untruthful with hospital staff about how the injury was sustained and the hospital staff notified law enforcement authorities," Luna said, adding that when Arcadia police went to the home, "what they discovered raised even more serious concerns."

The district attorney said Tuesday that the children were seated for hours a day in three different rooms called "Learning Centers" under the supervision of various nannies at the couple's home, which he called a "house of horrors." The couple kept a system of 32 motion-activated cameras in the various rooms in the Arcadia mansion, he said. Footage from these cameras went to a television near their desk that the couple used to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.

Hochman said the nannies were caught on video spanking, slapping or hitting the children. One nanny, Chunmei Li,  allegedly struck the 2-month-old baby in the head, the district attorney said. A $105,000 warrant for her arrest was previously issued, but she remains on the run, he said.
Xuan's attorney, Mitchell Krems, said: "My client is innocent. It is the nanny's wrongdoing who went on the run. He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family."

Melissa Brisman, an attorney for two of the surrogates involved in the case, told CBS News, "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system."
Brisman added that it's important surrogacy remains an option for those who need the help to become parents, but said there must "be adequate protections for those who enter the surrogacy system."
"We need to make sure bad actors don't ruin it for everyone else," she said.

On Tuesday, officials said the Arcadia Police Department requested assistance from the LA County Sheriff's Department in early September. A Los Angeles FBI spokesperson confirmed the FBI served a search warrant at the home, separate from a search conducted by the sheriff's department.
"We will continue to work together to pursue justice for all 21 children involved in this case," Luna said.

Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who carried two children for Zhang and Xuan, said after learning of their arrest, "I'm mad that everyone involved couldn't stop this so the kids wouldn't go through everything they went through. I'm just mad with the whole process, the whole thing. It's not just them."
"I trusted Silvia," she said.

title: Paramount closes $110 billion deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
summary: The merger unites two major movie studios, news operations CBS News and CNN and cable networks including Comedy Central and TNT.
story: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, uniting the movie studios behind "The Godfather" and the "Harry Potter" films into a media colossus rebranded as Skydance.
The merger also brings together the news outlets CBS News and CNN, major cable networks such as Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT and the streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who orchestrated the merger as CEO of Paramount Skydance, will lead the new company along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who was previously CEO of toy company Mattel.
In an email to employees, Ellison and Kreiz said the merger will allow the company to create a "stronger competitor, one with the scale to take on the biggest players in our industry."
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a separate statement from Skydance.
As part of the deal, Warner Bros. shareholders will receive the cash equivalent of roughly $31 per share, the company said.

The deal came together after Paramount settled a July lawsuit from a coalition of 12 state attorneys general and a separate lawsuit from the Writers Guild of America (WGA). Both had sued to block it on antitrust grounds.

Under the settlement agreement, Paramount pledged to produce 30 films in each of the first two years after the merger and is barred from selling or closing the Paramount or Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles for at least five years.

Paramount has also agreed to establish an editorial board to "help CNN and CBS maintain editorial independence," according to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office. WGA agreed to settle its lawsuit after Paramount reached a deal with the states.
Ellison and Kreiz said the company is targeting $6 billion in cost savings, a move that some in the media industry are concerned could lead to job losses.
"Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," the co-CEOs said in the email to Skydance employees.

title: The life and travels of an alleged Chinese agent in the U.S.
summary: A CBS News investigation reveals new details about the life and background of a California mom accused of conducting surveillance for China.
story: Three years before California realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang was arrested as an alleged Chinese agent, she showed up in San Francisco celebrating the visit of President Xi Jinping.
Zhang was photographed in 2023 wearing a red cap and marching on the street alongside the leader of a Chinese American organization with deep ties to the Beijing government's foreign influence arm.
Soon after the photo was taken, pro-Chinese Communist Party activists there began assaulting protesters of Xi's authoritarian regime — though there is no evidence Zhang was involved in any attacks.
The Orange County mother, 34, is now facing federal prosecution for allegedly surveilling the Taiwanese president's son in Washington last year at the direction of Chinese government officials.

The FBI said it has obtained her text messages with Chinese intelligence officials, plotting and executing a plan to secretly film Taiwan's first son, Lai Ting-yu, and his family in the Seattle suburb where they live.
Investigators even allege they have footage from a neighbor's security camera catching Zhang in the midst of her surveillance mission.

A CBS News investigation reveals the alleged agent's backstory bears striking similarities with infamous suspected Chinese spy Fang "Christine" Fang, who had an intimate relationship with disgraced congressman Eric Swalwell before fleeing to China in 2015 amid an FBI espionage probe.
Like Fang, Zhang attended the University of International Relations in Beijing, which is run by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's intelligence agency and secret police.
In a criminal complaint filed in a Los Angeles court, FBI counterintelligence special agent Kevin Holt wrote that the ministry "recruits heavily" from the university.
After moving to the U.S., Zhang studied at the University of Southern California and got her real estate license in 2016.

She built her business as a realtor with Irvine-based JC Pacific Corp over the next decade, listing over 130 properties, according to Zillow, with prices ranging from the hundreds of thousands to upwards of $8 million.
Zhang and her husband, a fellow realtor at JC Pacific, bought their six-bedroom, 6,030-square-foot home for $5.65 million in 2024, records show. They sold the property in June for $6 million.

Her Instagram page shows curated photos of Zhang in designer clothing, dining at expensive restaurants, taking trips around the U.S. and Canada, and shopping at luxury stores with a friend in Paris last year.
Similar to Fang, she became involved in advocacy groups and events for Chinese Americans.

In 2022 she attended an "entrepreneurship competition" for Chinese students with Chinese government consulate officials, and was honored at an event for "Chinese young elites in the United States" the same year where she was given a "young entrepreneur" award.
Her involvement in the All American Chinese Association brought her in contact with officials who had deep ties to the Chinese government.

AACA's leader, Cai Chenghua, was vice chair of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, a U.S. group so close to the Beijing government it had to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as an influence arm of the Chinese Communist Party.

In 2022 Cai helped organize a celebration of China's National Day at which the Los Angeles consul general Zhang Ping urged Chinese Americans to oppose "Taiwan independence" and support China's "complete reunification."
AACA bused in pro-China supporters to San Francisco for President Xi's visit in November 2023. Zhang was photographed alongside Cai, wearing matching red caps behind an AACA banner.

AACA board member Tian Jun is also a committee member in the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office, which became part of the Chinese government's United Front in 2018, according to research by Michael Lucci, a security consultant who helps protect U.S. institutions from Chinese influence through his firm, State Armor.
Cai has been photographed at several events with former Arcadia, California, Mayor Eileen Wang, who pleaded guilty to acting as a Chinese government agent in May.

"U.S.-based groups linked to the Communist Party's United Front through their key personnel keep coming up in federal foreign-agent cases," Jacqueline Deal, an adviser to State Armor, told CBS News."This is not a coincidence. The mission of these organizations is to help the Party and hurt the United States."

At a minimum, Deal said officers from these groups should have to register with the U.S. Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. That's the federal law Zhang is alleged to have violated by acting as a Chinese agent without registering as required.
Cai has not been accused of any wrongdoing or charged with any crime. He did not respond to a request for comment.
According to prosecutors, by 2025 Zhang had fully embraced a role as a Chinese government agent.
She traveled to China in January that year and met a government official and fellow graduate of the University of International Relations, the FBI affidavit said.

Two months later, the pair texted on Chinese messaging app WeChat about the address of a Taiwanese official who spoke out against the Chinese government, according to records obtained by a search warrant of Zhang's iCloud account, the FBI agent wrote.

She allegedly visited China again in June and met with a second Chinese official in the private room of a restaurant, where investigators believe she received her mission to surveil the Taiwanese president's son.
She later texted her alleged government handler: "I can take care of this thing."

After recording video of Lai and his family, she returned to LA without incident, according to the complaint. She was arrested while attempting to board a flight to Shanghai at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday.
She appeared in court on Monday dressed in the same designer workout gear she was wearing during the arrest.
Her family declined to comment.

"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, in a statement released Monday.
"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals," he said.

A spokesperson for the Taiwanese president told CBS News he condemns "such brutal acts of suppression, intimidation, and even harm to the freedom and democracy of people or their families, which are unacceptable in the civilized world."

"We thank the US judicial agency for their assistance and protection to our people," the spokesperson said. "Taiwan will continue to cooperate with all democratic allies to jointly combat illegal acts of cross-border repression."

The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not respond to CBS News' request for comment. A spokesperson  told NBC News,  "China has always opposed hyped-up accusations of 'China spying' that slander and smear the country."

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed by firing squad, Pentagon says
summary: The Trump administration has approved a plan to execute former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan — who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood — by firing squad, the Pentagon said.
story: The Trump administration has approved a plan to execute former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan — who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood — by firing squad, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday.
Parnell said on social media the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.
"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
CBS News has reached out to Hasan's attorney for comment.

According to an email sent to the families of the victims and obtained by CBS News Texas on Tuesday, the execution has been scheduled for Dec. 3. When CBS News Texas reached out to Fort Hood for comment, it was directed to Army headquarters.

A former Army psychiatrist, Hasan was convicted of murdering 13 people and injuring more than 30 in a 2013 court-martial. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was sentenced to death.
Hasan's case could mark the military's first execution of an American service member since 1961, when a soldier was hanged for raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl.
It would also mark a rare use of a firing squad. The method was used in South Carolina three times last year, marking the first firing squad executions since 2010.

The federal government typically uses lethal injection for civilian death penalty cases. Earlier this year, the Justice Department said federal officials should consider other methods, including firing squads, electrocution and lethal gas.

The decision by Hegseth comes after a lengthy appeals process for Hasan. He chose to represent himself at trial, and in an unusual course of events, he clashed with his own court-appointed standby attorneys, who worried that Hasan was intentionally seeking the death penalty.

Hasan asked the Supreme Court to review his case in 2024, arguing the judge violated his right to a public trial by clearing the public from the courtroom before discussing some of his issues with the attorneys. The high court declined to take up the issue last year.

title: Christa Pike is conscious, speaking after botched execution, attorneys say
summary: Christa Pike, a death row inmate who was subject​ to a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, is conscious and speaking from her hospital bed, her attorneys said Tuesday.
story: Christa Pike, a death row inmate who was subject to a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, is conscious and speaking from her hospital bed, her attorneys said Tuesday.
Pike survived the state's Sept. 30 attempt to execute her by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She has been hospitalized since.

In a statement Tuesday, her attorneys said that she was "conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," but noted that "her prognosis remains unclear" and "at a minimum" they "expect a long recovery."
They also said that "despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed."

Pike was given two lethal doses of pentobarbital, but according to media witnesses, the execution was canceled when it was determined she had not lost consciousness and still had a heartbeat. One media witness noted that she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.
One of her attorneys, Steve Ferrell, told "CBS Mornings" on Monday that doctors were working to clear her body of the pentobarbital and that she was on a ventilator.
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder of a former classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time of the crime, and 20 when she was sentenced in 1996.
Pike's execution was allowed to move forward last week after the Supreme Court denied a last-minute effort to halt it. She was set to be the first woman executed in the state in about two centuries.

In the wake of the failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said the state's prison chief, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, will resign. Lee also said that all remaining scheduled executions in the state this year have been canceled amid what he said would be a "third-party review" of the botched execution. Pike's attorneys have also filed a motion in Davidson County court requesting that all evidence related to the failed execution be preserved.

In that motion, her attorneys also claimed that during the execution, the corrections department team failed to realize that the IV lines had not been correctly placed "or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering" Pike's body.
Ferrell told "CBS Mornings" that her legal team would like to see her sentence commuted.
"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," Ferrell said.

title: Eva Marie Saint, "North by Northwest" star, dies at 102
summary: Eva Marie Saint won an Oscar for her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in "On the Waterfront." She bucked many Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career.
story: Academy Award-winning actor Eva Marie Saint, who starred in such classics as "On the Waterfront" and "North by Northwest," but also bucked Hollywood conventions throughout her lengthy career, has died. She was 102.
Her publicist, Jeff Sanderson, said she died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles, surrounded by family and loved ones.

A regal-looking blonde who ricocheted from playing sultry spies to Southern belles and Superman's stepmother, Saint made her motion picture debut opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan's "On the Waterfront" (1954). Saint played Edie Doyle, whose brother was murdered by thugs working for a mob boss running a longshoremen's union; her character becomes involved with Brando's pugilistic dockworker Terry Malloy.

Her performance earned Saint one of the film's eight Academy Awards. (She was only the fourth person to win a best supporting actress Oscar for their film debut.) On the night she received her award, she was visibly pregnant. "I may have the baby right here!" she said. (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

Saint married director-producer Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, and the couple stayed together for 65 years until his death in 2016. They had two children. Saint had made it clear that family was more important to her than her career.

"I had an agent once who wanted me to make many more movies," she told CBS' "Sunday Morning" in 2014. "I said, 'I can't. I can only do one a year, if that. I have children, young children.' And he said, 'Well, I guess you won't be a superstar.' And I said, 'Well, I guess not.'"
And what happened to that agent? "Fired him," she said.

She kept up her self-imposed limit on films; she also brought her extended family to the set of Otto Preminger's "Exodus" while filming in Cyprus and Israel. Despite not cranking out movies, Saint followed her Oscar win by appearing in many prestige projects, including "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "All Fall Down," "The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," and the eponymous TV miniseries based on "How the West Was Won." She also received five Emmy nominations, and won for the 1990 TV movie "People Like Us." At age 97, she appeared on a podcast series.

But perhaps her most memorable performance was as Eve Kendall, a mysterious blonde who crosses paths with Cary Grant's Roger Thornhill as he runs from murderous spies in the 1959 Alfred Hitchcock thriller "North by Northwest." Little does Thornhill realize that Kendall herself is a secret agent.
Saint said Hitchcock's direction to her playing a sexy spy was simple: "Three things: Lower your voice. Don't use your hands. And look directly into Cary Grant's eyes at all times," she recalled.

Hitchcock had a reputation for being tough on young female actors, but not Saint. "I found that he was such a wonderful director, gentleman, funny, courteous, but there are other actresses who don't feel the same way. I don't even want to hear stories about him," she said.
Though playing a femme fatale was new to her, Saint said she wasn't surprised upon watching her performance. "No. I don't think actors are surprised," she said. "I mean, that's what we do."
"Too innocent" looking

Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, Saint grew up in upstate New York, and attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio (where she was "Sweater Queen"). Originally planning to become a teacher, Saint began acting in student productions, and changed her career focus.

Moving to New York City, she trained at the Actors Studio with famed acting coach Lee Strasberg, and was hired for a production of "Mister Roberts" alongside Henry Fonda. But she was let go by director Joshua Logan; she found out it was because she was deemed "too innocent" looking. The actor who took her place was Jocelyn Brando (Marlon's sister).
Crushed, she was nonetheless determined not to let it dissuade her from pursuing an acting career.

When she was starting out, she told Variety in 2021, Saint and a fellow female actor would talk in a made-up language while riding the subway. "We were so frustrated about not getting jobs, so I suggested that we do something so people would notice us," she said. "When we'd start gabbing, we'd get a little audience. People would put down their papers and wonder, what language is that?"

Saint established herself in the early days of live television as a dramatic actor in plays on "Studio One," "Goodyear Television Playhouse," "GE True Theater" and "Philco Television Playhouse." She starred in the first TV production of Horton Foote's "The Trip to Bountiful," and repeated her role on Broadway, where she was spotted by Kazan, the "Waterfront" director.

He asked Saint to audition opposite Brando in an improvised scene. Upon entering the room, Brando put on a radio, and the two started dancing. "He did something to flip my skirt, and I was so embarrassed I cried a little bit afterward," Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2010. "But Kazan saw the chemistry, and he could see that it could work for the movie."
She said Brando was wonderful to work with.

"What was a little scary about him, which worked for me in the movie, was his perception of people that was so keen," she said. "He could look at somebody or talk with them and hone into what that person was all about. And he would mention it about people around us. So sometimes I would sit there and think, 'If he knows that about that person, he must know more about me than I know about myself.' It made me a little self-conscious, but I used that in the movie. He'd been out in the world and I had been at home protected, so I used that."
Following "Waterfont," Saint appeared on TV in a musical version of Thornton Wilder's "Our Town" with Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra, and also appeared onstage numerous theater productions.

But Hollywood beckoned, and the Oscar winner starred opposite such actors as Montgomery Clift and Elizabeth Taylor ("Raintree County"), Paul Newman ("Exodus"), Warren Beatty ("All Fall Down"), James Garner ("36 Hours"), Richard Burton and Taylor ("The Sandpiper"), Yves Montand ("Grand Prix"), Gregory Peck ("The Stalking Moon"), Bob Hope ("That Certain Feeling," "Cancel My Reservation"), and Tom Hanks ("Nothing in Common").
Other film credits included "Because of Winn-Dixie," "Don't Come Knocking" (with Sam Shepard), "Superman Returns" (as Martha Kent), and "Winter's Tale."

On TV she appeared in "The Best Little Girl in the World," "Moonlighting," the two-hander "Taxi!!" (opposite Martin Sheen), "The Last Days of Patton" (with George C. Scott), "I'll be Home for Christmas," "My Antonia," the 1996 TV miniseries "Titanic," and "Frasier."

And in recent years, Saint podcasted. She played Marisa Tomei's aunt in "The Bus Ride," a short play streamed on "The Pack Podcast." She said the feisty character, written by Eugene Pack, was compelling, calling his work "so honest."
"I've lived long enough to know what's honest and what isn't, and Eugene's plays are," she said. "They're charming, they're positive, but they're not saccharine."
Saint is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren and two great grandchildren, Sanderson's statement said.

title: Former Cornell frat members ask university to clear their names
summary: Some former Cornell University students say they are being falsely connected to a 2024 sexual assault​​ and targeted online.
story: A group of former Cornell University students say they are being falsely connected to the alleged 2024 fraternity house rape, and smeared and targeted online, and they want the college to say explicitly that they were not among men accused in the incident.

The former students, members of the Chi Phi fraternity who graduated in 2022 and 2023, say online sleuths have wrongly pegged them for harassment, leading to negative personal and professional consequences.
A lawyer for the group asked the school in a letter on Oct. 3 to clear them and others who graduated prior to the alleged assault.

"We understand that federal privacy law limits what Cornell may say about individual students, and we are not asking Cornell to identify anyone who was in the group chat," wrote attorney Adam Ford, referring to a Snapchat message thread from the night of the October 2024 incident. "We are asking for the opposite: a public confirmation as to who was not."

A woman identified as Jane Doe sued Cornell, the fraternity and several men who she says pressured her into taking the drug ketamine and sexually assaulted her. According to the suit, which was filed in September, a fraternity member sent a crude message to a Chi Phi Snapchat group chat suggesting that a woman was available for sex in a room in the frat house, leading to hours of assault.
The local district attorney did not bring criminal charges against anyone at the time. New York Attorney General Letitia James has now been appointed special counsel to investigate the case.

Ford's letter says none of the men he represents were in the group chat. While all had been previous members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity, they were not students at the time of the alleged assault.

Ford wrote that the men have been harassed in the days since a website devoted to exposing people associated with the rape posted their names under a list of former Chi Phi members. The messages they received, according to Ford, included threats like "I will find you," "you will never know peace" and "all 57 men of the fraternity deserve public execution."

The men's names have been removed from the website following a cease-and-desist letter sent on Oct. 2. A podcaster who indicated in a tweet that they were in the group chat also appears to have deleted the post after receiving a letter from Ford.

"Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave," Ford wrote in the letter, which was addressed to Brian White, Cornell's vice president and general counsel. "We believe Cornell is uniquely situated to correct the public record with a clear and unambiguous public statement that members of the Chi Phi fraternity who were not enrolled at Cornell during the fall of 2024 were not on the relevant 'Chi Phi Actives' Snapchat group chat."
A spokesperson for the school did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The men have also asked for individualized private letters "confirming that the University has information proving they were not members of the Chi Phi Actives group chat."
