title: FBI arrests woman at LAX accused of being Chinese agent
summary: Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was arrested on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
story: The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

title: Russia plays down reported plague lab death and says, trust us
summary: A Russian plague lab worker died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," officials say, in response to initial reports that she was exposed to the deadly bacteria during a lab accident.
story: Russia's government played down concerns Monday sparked by media reports that a female scientist in Siberia might have died of exposure to the plague after a lab accident.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov stressed that the state health watchdog known as Rospotrebnadzor was the "lead agency with expertise in this area," and he urged Russians to "listen to official information" from its "highly qualified professionals."
The researcher who died has been identified by Russian reports as Darya Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow.
Russian media initially reported that she broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and then died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said she died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.

The plague bacterium referred to by the reports is yersinia pestis, the same one that caused the Black Death that swept across Europe in the mid-1300s, killing an estimated 25 million to 50 million people. That pandemic, often referred to as the bubonic plague, was spread by fleas living on rodents and other animals in close proximity to — and in the same grim sanitary conditions as — people.
The pathogen, if untreated, can cause swelling, fever and death.

Shipilova, according to Russian media, died from the pneumonic plague, which is caused by the same bacteria but attacks the lungs and causes a fever and a cough that can turn bloody. Pneumonic plague can be transmitted from person to person, unlike bubonic plague, and can also be fatal.

The head of Russia's eastern Republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova died of the plague in a post on the state-backed messaging app MAX. He later edited the post to add the word "possibly," according to an independent regional Russian media outlet that operates in exile, Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal).
He was not the only Russian official to walk back their words on the story.
Local officials initially warned people not to visit the town of Shelekhov, where the scientist was hospitalized and later died, citing "unofficial information" about a human plague case.
The post was deleted less than two hours later, according to both Lyudi Baikala and Astra, another independent news website.
Since then, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has said it carried out "anti-epidemic measures" that included testing nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova.

The agency said some people had tested positive for colds or COVID, but that no pathogens causing dangerous infections were found. It also said there had been no accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and it attributed the scientist's death to "pneumonia of unknown origin."
A WHO spokesperson said that based on the unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general public appears to be low.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the reports of a suspected plague case in Russia were not cause for alarm, but "for focus."

"We know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided," he said. "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread."

But Rubio said, given "very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia," he did not believe it was "cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus, and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we're doing that."

title: Holly Madison blasts ‘puppet masters’ for Playboy girlfriends’ feud
summary: Holly Madison revealed she'd embrace manufactured drama on a "Real Housewives of Las Vegas" but refuses to be "puppeted" like on "Girls Next Door."
story: Holly Madison recalls feeling controlled by off-camera decision-makers during her time on "The Girls Next Door" and explains why she would approach reality TV differently today.
Holly Madison has no problem with reality TV drama — as long as everyone is in on the joke.

The "Girls Next Door" alum told Fox News Digital she would "100%" embrace manufactured conflict on a show like "Real Housewives of Las Vegas," but claimed manipulation by the "puppet masters" behind her former series contributed to lasting rifts among the cast.

For years, Madison had seemingly closed the door on reality television, previously saying she would never return after her experience on "The Girls Next Door." But with time and a different perspective on how manufactured drama could work, she admitted she has reconsidered that hard-line stance.

"You know what, I've changed my thought on that," the Grant a Gift Gala ambassador explained. "I would do manufactured drama if I was in on the joke. I always say that to Bridgette watching 'Girls Next Door,' I'm like, if we knew what the drama was and the three of us were gonna play it out on screen and not take it home with us, so to speak, when the cameras are done rolling, that would have been so much more fun to me than being manipulated from the puppet masters above."
HOLLY MADISON SAYS PLAYBOY MANSION FELT LIKE A 'SAFE HARBOR' AFTER SHE ENCOUNTERED HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE
Playmate Holly Madison, Hugh Hefner, Bridget Marquardt and Kendra Wilkinson promote "Girls Next Door" on June 12, 2007. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

"Some of us from the cast are still not speaking today because of things like that, so. I would actually do manufactured drama, 100%. I would throw down on like a 'Real Housewives of Las Vegas.' I just don't want to be puppeted again."
The former reality star also pointed to another major difference between the television landscape then and now: the audience.

"Editing's crazy," she noted. "But I also appreciate that viewers are a little more sophisticated now. I mean, back in the 'Girls Next Door' days, they could edit something to be not what it was. And everybody watching was like, 'Nope, that's your character. That's who you are.'"
WATCH: HOLLY MADISON SAYS SHE'D EMBRACE ‘MANUFACTURED DRAMA’ ON REALITY TV UNDER ONE CONDITION
‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR SADIE ROBERTSON HUFF ADMITS ‘FEARS’ OVER PUTTING HER KIDS ON REALITY TV
Former Playboy Bunny Holly Madison rose to fame on the hit reality TV series "The Girls Next Door" about the Playboy Mansion. (Michael Bezjian/WireImage)
There is one non-negotiable for the former Playboy model.
"I would never put my kids on TV, ever, ever, ever," she told Fox News Digital.

Madison shares a daughter, Rainbow, and a son, Forest, with ex-husband Pasquale Rotella. She said her kids know bits and pieces about her Playboy past, but the once-iconic brand barely registers with their generation.

"So it's all kind of vague, and they don't see it as like a bad thing. Like anytime it's brought up or mentioned, it's kind of laughed about," Madison added. "So I'm glad that whoever's bringing it to their attention or bringing it up — because it's not me or their dad — whoever's bringing it up is bringing it up like it's a positive or a cool thing or a funny thing. It's not like bad or shameful or gross or anything."
HOLLY MADISON EXPOSES HUGH HEFNER’S ALLEGED 'CULT-LIKE' TACTICS, 'WEIRD' GROUP SEX NIGHTS AT PLAYBOY MANSION
Holly Madison, Hugh Hefner and Bridget Marquardt attend a Hollywood event on Dec. 13, 2007. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic)

Madison became a household name through her years at the Playboy Mansion and her relationship with Playboy founder Hugh Hefner. She later moved to Las Vegas, headlined the stage production "Peepshow" and starred in her own reality series, "Holly’s World." Madison also became a bestselling author: her 2015 memoir, "Down the Rabbit Hole," debuted at No. 1 on The New York Times bestseller list.

But Madison’s perspective on those years has continued to evolve. An autism diagnosis later in life gave her a new framework for understanding everything from the people she gravitated toward to why she thrived in certain environments and struggled in others.
She was formally diagnosed with autism in 2023, although she had speculated for years she might be on the spectrum.

Holly Madison (right) moved into the Playboy Mansion in 2001 at age 21 and went on to become Hugh Hefner's longtime girlfriend. (Robert Mora/Getty Images)

"I understand some of the people I would gravitate to and some of decisions I made differently," she told Fox News Digital. "I always felt like not being able to connect with other people and not being able to connect with boys my age was some kind of like mystical fated thing. Like I'm just not meant to do this."
Madison said those struggles led her down different paths as she tried to navigate social situations she didn’t always understand.

"Sometimes I would look back and think, 'Oh, that person hated me and I could never figure it out.' And now I'm like — I kind of get it," she explained. "I think they were taking some of my mannerisms and some of [the] ways of communication the wrong way. So, it's just really opened everything up for me."
Holly Madison was the host and executive producer of Investigation Discovery's "The Playboy Murders." (Denise Truscello/WireImage)

Looking back, Madison said she better understands why her role at the Playboy studio suited her. Working with incoming Playmates gave her a clear framework: She could give them tours, explain how things worked and ask questions about their lives rather than having to navigate an unstructured social situation.
"So I can definitely see why I was thriving where I was thriving and why I was failing where I was failing," Madison said.

Madison’s own experience has also given her a personal connection to the autism community. She is now using her platform to support Grant a Gift Autism Foundation, a Southern Nevada nonprofit that provides resources and services to individuals with autism and their families.

She's returning as an Event Ambassador for the 16th annual Grant a Gift Gala, supporting Grant a Gift Autism Foundation, Ackerman Center — on Oct. 22.

"It's so helpful, you know, to give them some steps and some therapies and some things the kids can do," Madison explained. "And it's also important to remember that autism is such a spectrum. You know, there are families who are really struggling with kids that need a lot of support."
"So, I love being a part of that and being able to help with that."

MIRANDA LAMBERT SAYS SHE AND ELLA LANGLEY CLASHED WHILE MAKING HIT RECORD
Miranda Lambert said she and Carrie Underwood fought for their places in the country music industry. (Eric McCandless)

title: Michael Douglas reveals he made five phone calls to five women the day he chose Catherine Zeta-Jones
summary: Michael Douglas reveals in his memoir "One Helluva Ride" that he called five women in one day to prove his commitment to Catherine Zeta-Jones.
story: Michael Douglas discusses surviving stage 4 cancer, maintaining a lasting marriage and his close relationship with son Cameron. The Oscar winner has written a new memoir, "One Helluva Ride."
Michael Douglas didn’t just choose Catherine Zeta-Jones — he called five other women in one day to make sure she was the only one.

The two-time Oscar winner pulls back the curtain on his extraordinary life in his new memoir, "One Helluva Ride," revealing his struggle to escape his father Kirk Douglas’ towering shadow, his past affairs and drug use, his terrifying battle with stage IV cancer — and the highs and lows of his decades-long love story with the actress.

Douglas first fell head over heels for Zeta-Jones when she caught his eye in the 1998 movie "The Mask of Zorro." Douglas, who is 25 years older than Zeta-Jones, later came across an interview in which she said she liked older men. He thought he had a chance.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET

Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas attend the launch of the new Aston Martin DB12 at the Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes on May 24, 2023, in Cannes, France. In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," Douglas revealed that he broke up with five women before embarking on a romance with Zeta-Jones. (David M. Benett)
Douglas went on to meet Zeta-Jones at the Deauville Film Festival in France. As the evening came to an end, Douglas blurted out, "I'm going to be the father of your children."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"One Helluva Ride" by Michael Douglas is available now. (Grand Central Publishing)

Zeta-Jones wasn't exactly swept off her feet. She knew about Douglas’ reputation as a Hollywood womanizer and remained wary of his intentions. Douglas, however, was determined to convince her that this time he was serious.
Eventually, Zeta-Jones was willing to give Douglas a chance, but under one condition: he needed to be monogamous.
WATCH: MICHAEL DOUGLAS SHARES LESSONS ON CANCER, MARRIAGE AND FAMILY
"I'm not interested in dating you if you're dating other people," she told him. "You can either continue with them or end it and be with me."
That day, Douglas wrote, he made five phone calls to five women he was seeing who lived in different cities.
Catherine Zeta-Jones attends a photocall for Martin Campbell's movie "The Legend of Zorro" on Oct. 3, 2005, in Paris. "The Mask of Zorro" was released in 1998. (Getty Images)

"Just after my marriage, I had been seeing five other women," he wrote. "They knew I was recently separated and in the process of getting a divorce. I made sure they all lived in different cities, which felt like a respectful way to be nonmonogamous. None of them asked for a commitment or even asked what else I was up to. I am sure they were seeing other people, too."
Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones during the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on Nov. 21, 2025, in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images)
He told each woman he had met someone and could no longer see her. According to Douglas, "they all took it well."
The couple married in 2000. They welcomed their son, Dylan, that year, followed by their daughter, Carys, in 2003. Today, the couple split their time between New York, Mallorca and Santa Barbara.
Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones visit Children's Hospital for Wales in Cardiff, Wales, on June 20, 2006. (WireImage)
But their Hollywood love story hasn’t always been picture-perfect.

Carys Zeta Douglas, Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones attend the "Jeanne du Barry" screening and opening ceremony red carpet at the 76th annual Cannes Film Festival at Palais des Festivals in Cannes, France, on May 16, 2023. (WireImage)
In the book, Douglas wrote that in 2013, the couple went on vacation and, upon returning, "had a heart-to-heart" about their relationship.
Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas attend the 2019 Netflix Primetime Emmy Awards after-party at Milk Studios in Los Angeles, on Sept. 22, 2019. (Getty Images for Netflix)

"We had been married for more than a decade," Douglas recalled. "We had just gone through a period where a number of challenges came at us all at once. We decided to take some time apart. We still loved each other immensely, but we needed to make sure that being married was the right thing for all of us."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker finalized their divorce in 2000, after which he married Catherine Zeta-Jones. (Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images)

"The entire ordeal was incredibly difficult," Douglas wrote. "Catherine and I have a very intense, deep love for each other. And we love our kids dearly. We worked hard to make sure they understood that this wasn't their fault. It wasn't anyone's fault. I had learned the hard way that staying together for the children isn't always the right course of action. Sometimes you need to take a step back and make sure you're doing what's best for your whole family."
Douglas and Zeta-Jones had weathered an extraordinarily difficult stretch for their family.

Michael Douglas is seen here sitting down for his first exclusive television interview since his cancer treatments. Douglas announced his stage IV cancer diagnosis on Aug. 16, 2010, and he has been in remission and cancer-free since January 2011. (NBC Newswire/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

In 2010, Douglas was diagnosed with cancer. That same year, his eldest son, Cameron Douglas, was battling addiction and was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty to drug charges. At the same time, Douglas was embroiled in a legal dispute with his ex-wife, Diandra Luker, over proceeds from "Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps."
Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker were married for 23 years, from 1977 until their divorce was finalized in 2000. (Sygma via Getty Images)
In his memoir, Douglas acknowledged that the mounting pressure took a toll on his wife, writing that "all of that stress" was "heaped onto" Zeta-Jones.

Zeta-Jones and the couple’s two children, Dylan and Carys, stayed in the family’s home in Bedford, New York. Douglas rented another place nearby so he could still see the children. He and Zeta-Jones "spoke regularly, but not every day."

From left: Catherine Zeta-Jones, Michael Douglas and Carys Zeta Douglas attend the "Jeanne du Barry" screening and opening ceremony red carpet at the 76th annual Cannes Film Festival at Palais des Festivals on May 16, 2023, in Cannes, France. (Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images)
"Part of taking a break is actually taking a break, something Diandra and I had struggled to do productively," he wrote of his past marriage.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
From left: Dylan Michael Douglas, Michael Douglas and Cameron Douglas attend the Princess Grace Awards at The Pierre Hotel in New York City on Oct. 23, 2024. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
"It was hard on the kids, and they were so strong during the entire ordeal," Douglas wrote. "They knew that we both loved them more than anything, and their trust in us never wavered."
As Douglas navigated the separation, he wrote that he never gave up hope that he and Zeta-Jones would reconcile.
Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas attend the 17th Annual Night of Stars on Oct. 24, 2000, in New York City. The couple married Nov. 18, 2000, at New York's Plaza Hotel. (Getty Images)
"I love Catherine in a way that I have never loved any other woman," he wrote. "She's my wife, my best friend, and my life partner. I could never lose her."
Best supporting actress winner Catherine Zeta-Jones in the press room at the 75th Annual Academy Awards. She was pregnant with her daughter, Carys. (Joe Llano/WireImage)

"As Catherine and I were seeing each other more surrounding the kids — school functions, drop-offs, extracurricular activities — we realized we both missed each other enormously," he wrote. "Taking time away helped reignite the spark that had brought us together."
The couple reconciled in 2014.
Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas attend the "Entrapment" premiere at the Odeon cinema in Edinburgh, Scotland, on June 30, 1999. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

"Thank God we found our way back to each other," Douglas wrote. "Our marriage deserved a second chance. Today, our marriage is stronger than ever, and we recently celebrated our 25th wedding anniversary. We still love spending time together. We can play 18 holes or walk on the beach, or we can just sit on the couch all day long talking. After all these years, wherever we are in the world, Catherine Zeta-Jones is still an incredible date."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Catherine Zeta Jones and Michael Douglas stand on the second hole of The Old Course before the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship 2025 in St. Andrews, Scotland, on Sept. 30, 2025. (Getty Images)
After decades together, Douglas told Fox News Digital he has learned a major lesson about making a marriage last in Hollywood.

"Making that person, that partner, as special as 25 years later," he said. "Make her feel as special 25 years later as the first day you started wooing her. What happens sometimes, after a while, is compatibility, and we end up making more of an effort with strangers than the person closest to you. So, I think it really calls for mutual respect and a good sense of humor."
Michael Douglas attends the Women In Cinema event during the Red Sea International Film Festival 2024 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on Dec. 6, 2024. (Getty Images)
When asked what Zeta-Jones, 57, does that still makes him feel like the luckiest guy in the world, he didn't miss a beat.
Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas attend the "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania" UK gala screening at BFI IMAX Waterloo in London, England, on Feb. 16, 2023. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

title: Debra Messing says cost of living, subway violence pushed her to back Trump-endorsed Republican

story: Kennedy joins 'The Story' to react to actress Debra Messing’s endorsement of Republican Bruce Blakeman for New York governor. She discusses Messing’s criticism of New York City’s decline and the political shift among some Hollywood liberals.
Debra Messing defended her decision to support Trump-backed Republican Bruce Blakeman for governor of New York on Tuesday.

The "Will & Grace" actress wrote in a lengthy Instagram post that while she has been a Democrat her whole life and for years her focus has been on voting rights, the gay community and gun control, she is increasingly concerned about the quality of life in New York City.
"I still stand by every one of those principles," the 58-year-old said, adding, "What has changed is how I feel about the city and state I love dearly."
DEBRA MESSING DITCHES DEMOCRAT FOR TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN AS SHE SOUNDS ALARM OVER NEW YORK

"I know I’m not someone choosing between rent and groceries. But many of the people who make New York what it is: small business owners, teachers, nurses, and young people trying to start their lives here, are struggling with the rising cost of living, and policies like congestion pricing are making it difficult to afford," she wrote.
She said when the people who live in the city can’t afford to live there, "we risk losing part of what has long made New York an extraordinary place of opportunity."

title: Music legend slams LA festival after woman's body allegedly left in the crowd following her death
summary: Sheila E. says she was never told that Shari Sanders' body remained in the crowd at the Carson Jazz Festival until after her performance ended.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Sheila E. slammed festival organizers following the death of a woman at the concert whose body was allegedly left in the crowd until after her performance.
The legendary musician admitted she was heartbroken upon hearing how Shari Sanders died at the Carson Jazz Festival amid sweltering temperatures over the weekend in Southern California.
On social media, Sheila told her followers about a "very important" situation where a concertgoer died either "during or before" her performance.
ROD STEWART CONFIRMS FINAL TOUR AFTER HEART PROCEDURE AND HEALTH SCARES
Sheila E. slammed festival organizers after a woman's body was left in the crowd after she died during the sweltering Los Angeles heatwave. (Michael Loccisano)

The musician explained that it was "very hot that day" with temperatures soaring above 100 degrees in Southern California.

"When we got there at 7:30 a.m., people were already in line sitting in their chairs waiting to get in," she said before noting that organizers opened the grounds 30 minutes early to let attendees in.
She noted witnessing emergency crews "going through the crowds like crazy," while waiting with her band for her set at the festival.

"We were thinking, it's so hot outside ... maybe people were dehydrated, and we could see that through the window of the dressing room," she said. "We never got our sound check, so things were running late. Production wasn't there, stuff was just happening."

Sheila said that the bystander asked her if she was "OK" and she was "not responsive."

"That is uncalled ... that is not even uncalled for. It's devastating," she said. "I just want to say to the community, that I would have never – never gotten on stage if I would have known that her body was still sitting there with her family surrounding her."

title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning ‘On the Waterfront’ and ‘North by Northwest’ star, dead at 102
summary: Oscar winning actress Eva Marie Saint, who starred opposite Marlon Brando and Cary Grant, has died at 102 after a career spanning seven decades.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-and Emmy-winning actress who became one of the defining stars of Hollywood’s Golden Era, has died. She was 102.
Saint died Tuesday of natural causes at her Los Angeles home surrounded by family and loved ones, her representative confirmed to Fox News Digital.
The actress made an extraordinary film debut opposite Marlon Brando in the 1954 classic "On the Waterfront," winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress in her performance as Edie Doyle.

Directed by Elia Kazan, the landmark drama launched Saint onto the big screen after she had already established herself in television and on the New York stage. Her first movie role placed her opposite Brando at the apex of his fame.
POST MALONE, EVA MARIE SAINT AND OTHER CELEBRITIES WHO SHARE A BIRTHDAY WITH THE FOURTH OF JULY
American actress Eva Marie Saint paints from a sketchbook in a garden in the United States, circa 1955. (Archive Photos/Getty Images)

Five years later, Saint then firmly cemented her place in Hollywood's Golden Era history while starring opposite the legendary Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s "North by Northwest," playing mysterious "Hitchcock Blonde" Eve Kendall in the cult-classic 1959 thriller.

The role offered a striking contrast to the vulnerable, angelic young woman she portrayed in "On the Waterfront." As Hitchcock’s elegant and enigmatic leading lady, Saint became part of one of the British director’s most enduring films, sharing the screen with Grant in a movie remembered for its sweeping romance, suspense and iconic Mount Rushmore climax.
Saint’s two best-known films alone paired her with Brando, Kazan, Grant and Hitchcock, but represent only the start of a career that would stretch more than 70 years.

Over an incredible career spanning more than seven decades, Saint worked alongside some of Hollywood’s most celebrated leading men, including Montgomery Clift, Henry Fonda, Paul Newman, Gregory Peck, Richard Burton, Warren Beatty, James Garner, George C. Scott, Burt Lancaster and Tom Hanks.
OSCAR-WINNER BRENDA FRICKER, 'PIGEON LADY' FROM 'HOME ALONE 2,' DEAD AT 81
Cary Grant holds Eva Marie Saint in a scene from the film "North by Northwest," 1959. Grant wears a pale gray Oxford shirt by Brooks Brothers. (FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)

Her list of co-stars reads like a roll call of midcentury Hollywood. She appeared with Clift and Elizabeth Taylor in "Raintree County," Newman in "Exodus," Beatty in "All Fall Down," Burton in "The Sandpiper" and Garner in the racing epic "Grand Prix."

Other notable films featuring the actress included "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "Exodus," "The Russians Are Coming the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," "Nothing in Common" and, later in her career, "Superman Returns."

Saint was also a regular fixture of television and the stage. She earned five Emmy nominations, winning in 1990 for the miniseries "People Like Us," and appeared on Broadway in "The Trip to Bountiful" before director Elia Kazan cast her in "On the Waterfront."
SHELLEY FABARES, STAR OF 'THE DONNA REED SHOW' AND 'COACH,' DEAD AT 82
Eva Marie Saint at the 90th Academy Awards, which broadcast live on Sunday, March 4, 2018, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood. (Disney General Entertainment Con)

Her career had actually begun during the golden age of live television. Saint earned early Emmy nominations for Paddy Chayefsky’s "Middle of the Night" and a live television musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder’s "Our Town," in which she played Emily alongside Frank Sinatra and Paul Newman.

On Broadway, her performance in the Christian-themed "The Trip to Bountiful" earned her critical acclaim and caught Kazan’s attention. Saint's moves from radio and live television to Broadway and then an Oscar-winning movie debut uniquely placed her at the crossroads of several defining eras of 20th century American entertainment.

Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised in Albany and Delmar, New York, Saint attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio with plans to become a teacher before acting ultimately changed the course of her life.

She tried out for a university play at the suggestion of a drama professor, won the leading role and abandoned her original plan to become a schoolteacher. After graduation, she moved to New York City, studying at the American Theatre Wing and with Lee Strasberg at the Actors Studio.

Bowling Green later awarded Saint an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree and renamed its main campus theater the Eva Marie Saint Theatre. She returned to the Academy Awards as a presenter in 2009 and again in 2018, receiving a standing ovation from the stars gathered when she walked onto the stage at age 93.
PAUL ANKA SLAMS MODERN SINGERS, SAYS FRANK SINATRA WOULD HAVE 'THROWN A CHAIR'
1954: Actor Marlon Brando and Eva Marie Saint pose for a portrait on the set of the movie 'On the Waterfront' which came out in 1954. (20th Century-Fox/Getty Images)

Saint was married to director Jeffrey Hayden for 65 years until his death in 2016. She is survived by their two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren, Eli, Tyler, Molly and Stella, and two great-grandchildren, Arlo and Finley.

From the docks of "On the Waterfront" to the intrigue and glamour of "North by Northwest," Saint became an undisputed face of Hollywood history while building a body of work that endured long after that era had passed.

story: In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor admitted he had an affair with his "Basic Instinct" co-star, Jeanne Tripplehorn. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Michael Douglas is letting go of all his secrets in his new memoir.

According to Page Six, the 82-year-old actor disclosed in his new book, "One Helluva Ride, that he had an affair with a co-star almost 20 years his junior while filming the 1992 movie, "Basic Instinct."

While many at the time believed Douglas and his on-screen love interest, Sharon Stone, were having an affair in real life, the actor admitted in the memoir that it was actually actress Jeanne Tripplehorn with whom he was having the affair.
"The truth is, I fell very hard for Jeanne despite our nearly 20-year age difference," he said in the book. "In fact, I was ready to officially leave my wife for Jeanne. I was crazy about her."

At the time, Douglas was still married to his first wife, Diandra Luker, although he has said they were separated and living separate lives. Luker eventually filed for divorce in 1995.
He went on to say that his "relationship with Jeanne lasted through production," but that they "went our separate ways" once they were done making the film.
"But I will always think of her as an amazing actress and a truly terrific woman that I was very fortunate to spend time with," he added.

"Basic Instinct" follows Douglas' character, homicide detective Nick Curran, as he is seduced by a crime novelist and prime murder suspect, played by Sharon Stone. Tripplehorn portrayed police psychologist Dr. Beth Garner, who was also Curran's lover.

title: Richard Gere confronts Hollywood fame, ego and greed as 'dark clouds' that threaten inner peace
summary: Richard Gere reveals how more than 40 years of practicing Buddhism helps him battle ego, greed and jealousy in his decades-long Hollywood career.
story: Richard Gere reflects on the values that shaped his life and explains why kindness, compassion and being of service to others can lead to greater happiness. The actor serves as executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness."
Richard Gere has spent decades in Hollywood, but he hasn’t let fame go to his head — at least not without a fight.

The actor serves as an executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness," which explores the Dalai Lama’s teachings and the pursuit of lasting joy. Gere has practiced Buddhism for more than 40 years.
Asked how he keeps fame and ego in check after decades in Hollywood, Gere admitted he isn’t immune.
TIM ROBBINS TURNS TO AYAHUASCA AFTER FEELING 'CONSUMED BY ANGER' OVER CANCEL CULTURE
Richard Gere attends the screening of the film "Wisdom of Happiness" during the BCN Film Festival at Cinemes Verdi on April 29, 2025, in Barcelona, Spain. (2025 Xavi Torrent)

"Everyone goes through that," the 77-year-old told Fox News Digital. "Everyone has the forces of greed, anger, self-cherishing, impatience, jealousy, the whole gamut. Everyone has that. So I think from Buddhist training and looking at these afflictive emotions and seeing where they’re coming from, they’re not innate in me. They’re kind of add-ons to basic clarity of the mind."

"It’s said that the mind is clear and knowing, so clear, vast, no limits," he said. "It has a sense of knowing, wisdom. The other stuff is just kind of add-ons, like dark clouds coming through. They come, and they go."
Richard Gere wears a tuxedo in New York, circa 1970. (Getty Images)
Gere also isn’t looking to Hollywood for happiness. The longtime leading man has learned that the perks only go so far.
WATCH: RICHARD GERE SHARES THE LIFE LESSON THAT BRINGS HIM HAPPINESS

"Well, clearly, happiness and peace [don’t] come from the outside," he explained. "It comes from inside all of us, and it’s there. You don’t have to create that. But I think it’s removing the bad habits, removing the causes that make us feel bad ultimately. But we’re in control of our experience for sure. We’re responsible for it. If you don’t like the way things are, you change it. And all things are changeable. They’re changing all the time anyhow. Probably when we fight the change is when we feel the worst."
For Gere, that also means questioning how much material success really matters.
Richard Gere prays during a visit to the Chogye Buddhist temple in Seoul on June 21, 2011. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"Well, what’s really important? Is it what I own or what I am?" Gere said. "I’m not going to get anything from the outside that is permanently going to make me happy."
The Dalai Lama and actor Richard Gere stand following a press conference at Yale College. (Getty Images)
"Momentarily, yes, like a piece of chocolate, but that’s not permanent, is it?" he joked.
Gere has also found happiness far from the spotlight. These days, the star splits his time between Spain and upstate New York.
Alejandra Gere, Richard Gere and his son Homer Gere attend "The Agency" premiere in New York City on Nov. 21, 2024. (Getty Images for Paramount+)

"Well, Spain is my wife’s country, so she gets super happy there," he said with a smile. "And I’ll tell you when my wife’s super happy, I’m super happy. And I grew up in the Northeast. I feel very close to that. And my early family memories, and my grandfather’s farm in Pennsylvania, I think, had a huge impact. It still does."

Alejandra Silva and Richard Gere attend Paramount+'s "The Agency" New York premiere at the Museum of Modern Art on Nov. 21, 2024. (WireImage)
Gere and his wife, Spanish publicist Alejandra Silva, have two sons together. Silva also has a son from a previous relationship, while Gere shares his eldest son, Homer, with ex-wife Carey Lowell.

"My first son is 26 now," Gere said. "And I talked to him about what he’s going through right now. And I remember myself as a 25-year-old, 26-year-old person. Of course, my concerns were different. I certainly was more susceptible to what people said and thought about me and about anything else. And frankly, I don’t care that much about it right now, what anyone thinks or says."

Richard Gere and his mother, Doris Gere, attend the 19th annual American Museum of the Moving Image Benefit at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York City. (WireImage for NBC Universal Photo Department)

Looking back, Gere recalled growing up in "an extraordinary Christian family" with roots in a small town in Pennsylvania. His father, Homer Gere, spent his childhood milking cows, and both his parents instilled in him the importance of helping others — values he carried with him when he discovered Buddhism in his 20s.
Richard Gere and Vicki Sue Robinson appear on Broadway in November 1971. (Getty Images)

"I grew up with that imprint, I think, from my dad and my mom, but there was something about Buddhism that kind of went beyond that and was willing to explore the larger questions," Gere said. "What is reality? What am I? What is a human being?"
"Am I capable of much greater things than just worrying about myself?" he continued. "And certainly, Buddhism wanted to engage those things [for me]."
Richard Gere and Julia Roberts on the set of "Pretty Woman," directed by Garry Marshall. (Touchstone Pictures/Silver Screen Partners IV/Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
But the lessons Gere learned from farmers have never left him.

It doesn’t make you happy when the rain doesn’t come, or it comes too much, but the forces of the universe are just the way they are. And along with it, hard work."
"Farmers work really hard," Gere said. "I still have the kerosene lantern that my grandfather used. He would get up at four o’clock in the morning and go do the first milking of the cows."

Richard Gere kisses the Dalai Lama's hand during a prayer ceremony celebrating his 90th birth anniversary at the Main Tibetan Temple in McLeod Ganj, near Dharamsala, on July 6, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)
Gere said he sees that same work ethic in the Dalai Lama.

The Dalai Lama of Tibet presents actor Richard Gere with a traditional Buddhist prayer shawl during ceremonies on the West Front Plaza of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2007. (Getty Images)
"He still gets up at 3:30 in the morning, does his practice, works on his mind, works on his heart, works on his motivation, purifies himself every day," Gere said.

"He’s a human being, and he continues, as I said, to work on himself," he continued. "If we want to achieve what he’s achieved, to become really such an extraordinary, genuine person, we’ve got to do the work."
Richard Gere discovered Buddhism in his 20s. (Getty Images)
Gere said his connection to "Wisdom of Happiness" became deeply personal after he and Silva first watched the film together in New York.

Richard Gere and Alejandra Silva married in April 2018. (Pablo Cuadra/Getty Images)

Richard Gere receives the International Award during the 39th Goya Awards ceremony at the Granada Conference and Exhibition Center in Granada, Spain, on Feb. 8, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)

title: Dolph Lundgren says he 'always understood' Sylvester Stallone due to similar abusive childhood
summary: Dolph Lundgren says a shared abusive childhood helped him understand Sylvester Stallone in ways few others could across their 40-year friendship.
story: Lundgren reflects on his longtime bond with Stallone, crediting his 'Expendables' role with reviving his career and saying their shared experiences helped them understand each other.
Dolph Lundgren believes his shared abusive childhood helped him better understand Sylvester Stallone throughout their 40-year friendship.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Lundgren – who recently released his documentary "Dolph: Unbreakable" – explained the gratitude he has for the "Rocky" star after he "resurrected" his career.

"I think part of what's kept it going is I always have been very grateful to him and loving towards him. We've had our ups and downs, but I think, you know, he's discovered a lot of new talent and I think some of them perhaps haven't been as grateful maybe as some others, and I've always paid my respects to him because he's responsible not just for 'Rocky IV' but 'The Expendables.' I did four of those movies, which resurrected my career," Lundgren began.
Sylvester Stallone and Dolph Lundgren have had a friendship that has spanned four decades. (Kiyoshi Ota/Getty Images)

"We have daughters; he has three, I got two. And you know if you think about it, who can you ... if you're an action star, who had an abusive childhood, who has three daughters, who has a ton of injuries ... Who can understand you? There's not that many people you can talk to," Lundgren said.
The star explained that there is only Arnold Schwarzenegger left that could possibly understand his and Stallone's upbringing and life story.

story: Andrew Lownie, author of "Entitled," argues Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor worsened his own crisis and believes new Epstein-related details could still emerge.
Former Prince Andrew isn't waiting quietly for the police investigation into him to play out.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launched a legal challenge over searches of his homes following his February arrest.

Mountbatten-Windsor asked the court to rule on whether Thames Valley Police lawfully searched his homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate, according to The Daily Telegraph. A hearing will be held Thursday.

title: Engelbert Humperdinck says he ‘went through hell’ rejecting 'casting couch' advances early in career

Engelbert Humperdinck is reflecting on the dark side of trying to make it in the music industry, claiming he was repeatedly subjected to unwanted advances from talent agents early in his career.
During a recent episode of "The Engelbert Humperdinck Show," the 90-year-old British singer opened up about the struggles he faced while pursuing a music career in his early 20s.

Humperdinck recalled that he began traveling from his hometown of Leicester, England, to London in the late 1950s in hopes of establishing himself as a singer. He said that at the time, his older sister was able to give him just enough money to spend one night in a hotel while he visited talent agents.

Humperdinck said that talent agents repeatedly made unwanted advances toward him. (Bettmann Archive)

"She treated me very well. I ate very well during that six months, you know," Humperdinck recalled.

title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard launches anti-bullying campaign after sudden death of partner

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard is turning her "pain into purpose" after the sudden death of her partner, Kenan "Ken" Urker.
Urker died at his Louisiana home on his birthday Thursday, Oct. 1, Fox News Digital confirmed. He was 34.

Blanchard, 35, explained that Urker experienced "an overwhelming amount of online scrutiny" prior to his death, and pleaded with her social media followers to sign an anti-bullying petition in his honor.
GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD’S PARTNER, KEN URKER, FOUND DEAD INSIDE HIS LOUISIANA HOME: SHERIFF

Blanchard claimed that "reports were made across multiple platforms," but noted that "far too often, the response was simply: 'No violation.'"

"Kenan’s Law is about changing the way social-media platforms handle repeated reports of harassment," she wrote. "One post viewed alone may not tell the whole story—but hundreds of posts, videos and comments directed at one person can reveal a pattern that deserves meaningful review."

title: Matthew McConaughey says Woody Harrelson’s wild antics include 2 am visits, inviting strangers on vacations
summary: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson share outrageous stories from their decades-long friendship, including a possible DNA test revelation.
story: McConaughey said his "hands couldn't keep up with my mouth" as he tried to sing and play music at the same time in his new film, "The Rivals of Amziah King."
Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson's friendship has put both of them in some wild situations.
While promoting their new show, "Brothers," the two actors, and close friends, have shared many anecdotes from their years-long friendship, which have sent the internet buzzing.

Whether it be finding out they might be brothers to Harrelson surprising McConaughey in bed in the middle of the night, these two Hollywood icons have made it clear they have an interesting friendship.
Harrelson and McConaughey have shared many crazy stories from their years-long friendship. (Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV via Getty Images)
Here are some of the most outrageous stories the two shared during recent interviews.
MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY'S PIECE OF RELATIONSHIP ADVICE THAT KEEPS HIS MARRIAGE TO CAMILA ALVES STRONG
Late-night surprise
McConaughey shared Harrelson once climbed into his bed at 2 in the morning. (Shea Kastriner/USTA via Getty Images)
During an appearance on the "Glass Half Full" podcast, McConaughey described some of the oddities that come with being Harrelson's friend, saying "he's never gone through a front door in his life."
He explained that no matter how long it has been since they last saw each other, Harrelson has "never called or sent a message" to make plans, adding, "he just shows up."

"We hadn't seen each other for a year at the time when I was living out in LA. I hadn't seen him for a year. Guess my introduction to him," he said. "My wife goes 'ah.' And I go, 'Woah.' Two in the morning, wake up, Woody's in between us in bed! He had jumped the fence, picked the window, snuck in, and got in bed with us."
When host Craig Melvin told Harrelson that "people have been shot for less," the actor replied, "Well, I was hoping he didn't have a gun."
"But what a good way to wake up a friend, you know what I mean, and get to be next to Camila [Alves, McConaughey's wife]," Harrelson added. "Like, that was nice. She was warm to me."
Anniversary confusion
Harrelson and McConaughey have different accounts of when they first met. (David M. Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images)
When speaking to Melvin, the celebrity duo also shared how they first met, although they admit they have different recollections.
McConaughey admits Harrelson "believes we've known each other one year longer" than he does, because "I don't remember the first time we met."
He blames it on the idea that they began taking shots together at 1 p.m., but when Harrelson corrected him on a detail in the story, McConaughey told him, "I don't remember. You tell me."

"I already knew of him and I liked him from a distance," Harrelson said. "And then I met him, and I'm like, 'Hey, let's do a shot,' and he's like, 'Man, I got a lot of work to do today.' I said, 'One shot's gonna stop you from all the work you got?'"
McConaughey then chimed in adding, "Hence, I don't remember meeting that day. It doesn't sound like that was the beginning and the end of the story."
Living on the edge
McConaughey once witnessed Harrelson do a handstand on the edge of a canyon. (Gary Miller/FilmMagic)
While telling Melvin about Harrelson's many talents, McConaughey casually mentioned that the actor once "did a handstand 18 inches away from the edge of the Grand Canyon."

"The stuff this guy pulls off because he didn't know better is still amazing," McConaughey said. "Most people do that stuff when they're a kid, and they lose it as they get older, because you know better. This kid, what are you, 60 what now... 65 and he's still doing handstands on the edge of the Grand Canyon."
While Harrelson tried to downplay the achievement by saying he was farther away than McConaughey is saying and that it wasn't the Grand Canyon, the "Dallas Buyers Club" star continued to praise him.
"I'm probably exaggerating less than from the edge on his hand, the Grand Canyon," McConaughey said. "The photographer freaks out. Never got a picture of it."
He added that had the photographer been able to take a photo, "it would have been the most epic shot."
Vacation antics
Harrelson once invited strangers to join him and McConaughey on vacation. (Chloe Kern/FilmMagic)
While promoting the new show, the two actors also sat down with Conan O'Brien on his podcast, "Conan O'Brien Needs A Friend."

During the interview, McConaughey shared an unbelievable story about the time Harrelson met a couple on their honeymoon while waiting for his luggage at baggage claim in Greece, and invited them to stay with him and McConaughey in the house McConaughey had rented for them and their families.

"You have a consistent habit of having an open heart and inviting people into your future life or yours or mine," McConaughey told Harrelson during the interview. "He's doing this routinely. He's, he's very consistent. We go on a Greek holiday and my family… we rent the place... We rent the place and they… we fly over, but they get there before us and we show up and there's two people sitting on the tailgate of a truck right in front of our rental."

He went on to say that at first he thought it was Harrelson and his wife Laura, but soon found out it was two strangers who told him, "We met Woody and Laura at the airport getting our luggage and… they're great."
When he confronted Harrelson, who had already claimed the primary bedroom in the rental, he told him, "They're great, man. They're going to be with us for a week."
Break-in
McConaughey shared that Harrelson would often break into his home and sometimes stay for months at a time. (Todd Williamson/NBC via Getty Images)
When speaking with People, McConaughey expanded on the idea that Harrelson would show up at his home "unannounced," calling it "one of Woody's great traits."

"He never comes through a front door. And he’ll swing by for an hour to say, ‘Howdy!’" McConaughey said. "It might turn into, ‘I’ve moved in for three months.’ It’s a beautiful trait how he makes himself at home."

"There are times when I’m like, ‘Man, Woody, I need some space,’ and my whole family’s like, ‘No, don’t let Woody go. We’ve been staying up later having more milkshakes,’ whatever," McConaughey said. "The laughter’s been in the house a while."
Brothers?
Harrelson and McConaughey found out there was a chance they may be brothers. (Apple TV press site)

"In Greece a few years ago, we’re sitting around talking about how close we are and our families and et cetera and my mom is there. And she says, ‘Woody, I knew your dad,’" McConaughey told Kelly Ripa on her podcast in 2023.

title: Robert Blake’s son returns to restaurant tied to family tragedy for new murder mystery
summary: Noah Blake opens "A Killer Night in Studio City" at Vitello's, confronting decades of pain tied to his father Robert Blake's infamous trial.
story: Actor Noah Blake returns to Vitello’s with a new murder mystery show. The "Teen Witch" alum says it marks a personal step toward healing and forging an identity beyond his family’s past.

Twenty-five years after Vitello's became part of a painful chapter in his family's history, Noah Blake has returned to the restaurant to direct and star in a fictional murder mystery, describing the production as part of his healing journey.
The "Teen Witch" alum's "A Killer Night in Studio City," a noir-inspired immersive theater production set in 1958, opened at the famed Italian restaurant on Sept. 15.

"When I was first approached about this, of course, there was this little bit of ... and then I was like, 'Wait, what am I doing? Of course, I should do this,'" Blake told Fox News Digital. "This is a chance for me to, not rewrite history, but to create a new page and to create a new connection and a new relationship for me with this place, for my name with this place, for my family with this place."
ROBERT BLAKE DEAD AT 89

Noah Blake (right) stars in "A Killer Night in Studio City," which is described as "an immersive murder mystery where classic Hollywood glamour collides with scandal, ambition, romance, and murder." (Wes Chappell)

"I've got a four-year-old son," Blake said. "I want him to be able to go there and enjoy Vitello's as he's grown up, God willing, as long as Vitello's is there. And I don't want him to ever feel funny. I want him to think about, 'Oh, Vitello's, that's the place where daddy did that fun show.' Not this other stuff. I'm not trying to minimize that tragedy, but it wasn't my tragedy, and it was a cross that I've had to bear and still will probably for the rest of my life."
"A Killer Night in Studio City" is held inside The Velvet Martini Lounge inside Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

Blake said Vitello's was a regular gathering place for his family while he was growing up, but he stayed away for decades. He eventually returned and agreed to stage the production there, saying he wanted to reclaim positive memories of a place he had loved.
Vitello's Restaurant in Los Angeles is seen here on May 5, 2001. (Getty Images)

"I want to go and do something in this space that is creative, that is fun, that is exciting, where people come and laugh and gasp and have a great time," he explained. "Some people may not even know [what happened] and the people who do might be curious and go, 'Oh, that has nothing to do with anything, and I had a great time.'"
WATCH: NOAH BLAKE SAYS RETURN TO SITE TIED TO FAMILY TRAGEDY IS ‘FULL CIRCLE’
The history Blake is trying to move beyond dates back to 2001, when his father Robert Blake's wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed after the couple had dinner at Vitello's.

The actor was acquitted of murder in 2005 in connection with Bakley's killing. Bakley was shot and killed while sitting in Robert's car near the restaurant. A civil jury later found him liable for her death and ordered him to pay Bakley's family $30 million, prompting him to file for bankruptcy, according to The Associated Press.
Robert Blake in a scene from the 1967 movie "In Cold Blood." (Dukas/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
An appeals court later reduced the award to $15 million, after which the parties reached a confidential settlement. Robert died in 2023 at 89.

Robert Blake, star of the 1970s show "Baretta," stands in court with his attorney M. Gerald Schwartzback on Sept. 17, 2004, for a pretrial conference. Blake was accused of murdering his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, who was found shot dead in her car in Los Angeles in May 2001. (Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
Rose Lenore, Bakley's daughter with Robert, feels differently about the production. She told Fox News Digital that Vitello's remains too painful for her and others who loved her mother.

"I think him doing it at Vitello's is upsetting for me and anyone who loved Bonny," she said. "And there were quite a few people who did. She left behind three children, plus me. She also left behind a sister, my aunt, who misses her dearly. And so, to have Robert Blake's son do any show at Vitello's, let alone a murder mystery show, I find that to be insensitive and upsetting."
Bonny Lee Bakley, 44, was murdered on May 4, 2001. (ZUMA Press/ZUMA Archive / Shutterstock)

"I don't even care what the show is about," Lenore said. "I'm also not here to invalidate anyone's healing journey, if that's what this is for him. But I also think it's my moral obligation to stand up for what I believe in. I would still be upset if he was doing anything else. And for Noah to be doing a happy, fun show — I think it's in poor taste."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Rose Lenore Blake attends the Los Angeles screening of "Happy Anniversary" at LOOK Dine-In Cinemas Glendale in Glendale, California, on Jan. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

"I'm not wishing any harm on Noah," Lenore continued. "I wish him well in his life and career. But it would be hard for me to stay silent on something like this. It would be hard for me to stay silent about my mother."

Responding to Lenore's criticism, Blake wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital, "I have my own deeply personal reasons for doing this play. Vitello's was a place that I loved my entire life. Over time, that place became the physical embodiment for me of a much larger and devastating chapter of my life — one thing that I had nothing to do with, but whose consequences I have had to endure for years."
Noah Blake is seen here with his father Robert Blake during happier times. (Courtesy of Noah Blake)

"Choosing to walk back into that space now and create something uniquely mine — something lighthearted and entertaining that people are enjoying — is part of my own healing journey," he wrote. "It's about taking a place that had come to represent something painfully dark in my life and allowing it to represent something else. I'm not erasing history or rewriting it. I'm simply adding a new page to it, and I don't ask or expect anyone else to sign off on what I need to do to heal."

Actor Robert Blake and his son Noah Blake pause in front of the coffin bearing Bonny Lee Bakley on May 25, 2001, during a funeral ceremony in Los Angeles. Behind them are Robert Blake's assistant, Earle Caldwell, and an unidentified woman. (Getty Images)

"Rose is absolutely entitled to her feelings," Blake continued. "I've been there for her many times over the years, and I care for her. She chose to express her feelings about this publicly, which certainly wouldn't have been my choice and still isn't. I would much rather have had a private conversation with her. I've reached out and asked her to call me so that we could talk about this, and that conversation has yet to happen. But that door remains open for her."
Blake said returning to Vitello's has also forced him to revisit his complicated relationship with his late father.

Noah Blake (left) told Fox News Digital he hopes to one day make a documentary exploring his father Robert Blake's case, sitting down with those who knew the actor in an effort to better understand what happened the night his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed. (WireImage)

"I don't think people really realize when something like that happens, how many lives are impacted in such a profound way," he explained. "I had to wrestle with who my father really was for everything I thought he was or knew or saw him as. Did he do this thing? Was he really capable of this? Was he that far gone? Was my father this monster?"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Actor Robert Blake speaks exclusively to Barbara Walters from the Los Angeles County Jail, where he is being held without bail on charges of killing his wife, Bonnie Lee Bakley. Blake said he did the interview for his then-3-year-old daughter, Rosie. His first and only televised interview from jail aired on "20/20" on Wednesday, Feb. 26, 2003. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"It's tough because it makes you question a lot. 'What is my genetic makeup?' It was years of intense scrutiny, and it was impossible to live my life, and for other people as well. It's not cool to know that this guy's son had a nervous breakdown and couldn't leave his house for six months and was having panic attacks and night sweats and was incapable of functioning."
Robert Blake poses with his children Delinah and Noah at the Emmy Awards in Pasadena, California, in September 1977. (Getty Images)

"There were moments my father could be a very loving, kind, decent, generous human being," he said. "And there were times when he could just be an absolute f---ing monster and just the worst kind of selfish and menacing and threatening."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"A Killer Night in Studio City" is running through Halloween. (Wes Chappell)
Before his death, Robert fiercely denied murdering Bakley.

For Blake, returning to the restaurant carries a meaning beyond the fictional story he says he wants to tell. While he recognizes the connection others may make to his family's past, Blake stressed he does not want that history to define him.
Noah Blake told Fox News Digital he wants to create new memories at Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

"... I live my life as me," he said.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Shingles rates fall off a cliff among some Americans as researchers reveal likely reason
summary: Epic Research analyzed 85 million health records and found shingles rates dropped 62% among younger adults eligible for childhood chickenpox vaccination.
story: Neurologist Dr. Ajeet Sodhi breaks down research linking the shingles vaccine to a reduced risk of dementia, while stressing that the findings show an association, not proof that the vaccine treats dementia.
Shingles rates have dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s.
That’s according to a major study led by Epic Research, which analyzed the electronic health records of more than 85 million adults.
The biggest drop was between people born from 1991 to 1995 and those born from 1996 to 2000.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS

"Shingles is caused by a virus that is harbored in the peripheral nerves — varicella-zoster, the same virus that causes chickenpox — which can remain dormant and later reactivate, particularly during stress or other decreased immune responses, resulting in a shingles risk," Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, told Fox News Digital.
Shingles rates dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s. (iStock)
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease.
The study period was between January 2017 and June 2026, with the findings published on Oct. 2, 2026.
CANCER VACCINE PREVENTS DEADLY MELANOMA FROM RETURNING OR SPREADING IN LANDMARK TRIAL

Overall, shingles was found to be much more common in older adults. About 182 out of every 10,000 people born between 1968 and 1975 were diagnosed with the condition, compared with just seven out of every 10,000 born between 2006 and 2008.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Shingles diagnoses rise steeply with age, but the newer signal is a sharp drop that begins with people who were eligible for the childhood chickenpox vaccine in the mid-1990s," study author Kersten Bartelt, a research clinician in Verona, Wisconsin, told Fox News Digital.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease. (iStock)

If the trend continues as vaccinated groups grow older, it would suggest that childhood chickenpox vaccination could offer a lasting benefit in reducing shingles, "which is something continued follow-up and research will clarify," Bartelt added.

Siegel agreed that this data aligns with previous research showing that by preventing the initial infection via the chickenpox vaccine ("or causing a very mild version of a live virus vaccine") the risk of shingles is significantly reduced.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
He noted that the vaccine uses a weakened form of the virus, which is much less likely to reactivate later in life and cause shingles.
There were some limitations of the study, including that the researchers did not determine whether individual patients had actually received the varicella vaccination during childhood.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"This is a descriptive, observational study, so it shows associations rather than cause and effect," Bartelt said.
Healthcare disruption due to the COVID pandemic in 2020-2021 could have also affected diagnosis rates and skewed the results, the researchers noted.

A doctor noted that while people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk. (iStock)
Future studies are needed to confirm a link between childhood vaccination histories and long-term shingles outcomes.

"People should continue to follow established vaccine recommendations and talk with their clinician about the shingles vaccine when they're eligible," Bartelt advised. "It's also a reminder that shingles can occur in younger adults, so anyone with a painful, blistering rash should seek timely evaluation."

While people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, Siegel said he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends shingles vaccination for adults 50 and older, as well as certain immunocompromised adults 19 and older, including people who previously received the varicella vaccine.

title: People who live to 100 have 3 drinks in common, longevity expert says
summary: Dan Buettner highlights how blue zones residents drink water, black coffee and red wine with resveratrol to support long-term health goals.
story: Red wine gets plenty of criticism, but it still appears in some blue zone diets. Coffee may also support healthy aging. Yet the top longevity drink is much simpler, according to longevity researcher Dan Buettner.

In the world’s "blue zones" — regions such as Sardinia, Italy, and Okinawa, Japan, known for unusually high concentrations of long-lived residents — researchers have studied dietary and lifestyle habits for clues to healthy aging and longevity.
In a recent video post, longevity researcher Dan Buettner highlighted three beverages commonly consumed in blue zones — and studies offer some clues about how each may affect health and longevity.
No. 1: Purified water
Buettner ranked water first among his three longevity drinks.
FILTERED WATER AT SPECIFIC AGES COULD ADD MONTHS TO YOUR LIFESPAN DECADES LATER, NEW STUDY FINDS

"The indisputable, best thing you can drink to live to 100 [is] water," he stated. "People in blue zones are drinking six to seven glasses of water. You want to make sure it is purified water. Water helps lower your blood pressure, helps keep your blood thin and keeps you hydrated."
Research from the National Institutes of Health indicates that proper hydration helps prevent cellular degradation, lowers the risk of chronic heart conditions and supports healthy aging. (iStock)

Research from the National Institutes of Health has linked better hydration with healthier aging, including lower risks of chronic disease and premature death, although researchers noted that the findings do not prove cause and effect.
Other health experts note that adequate water intake supports kidney function, helps regulate blood pressure and keeps blood circulating effectively.
Coffee consumption has been associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's disease. (iStock)
No. 2: Black coffee
Coffee consumption is another daily habit highlighted by Buettner, who said it is associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Drink it black, one to two cups a day, quit by noon, it'll help you live longer," he added.
Routine coffee intake has been associated with reduced risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions. (iStock)

Coffee contains antioxidants and polyphenols, plant compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-inflammatory effects. Routine coffee consumption has also been associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Limiting added sugars and heavy creams can help avoid extra calories, while consuming caffeine earlier in the day may reduce its impact on sleep.
No. 3: Red wine
Residents in blue zone areas, like Sardinia, often consume small amounts of red wine during meals.
Buettner acknowledged that red wine's place in a longevity-focused diet is "controversial."
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the Blue Zones, and it seems to add years to life," Buettner said. (iStock)
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the blue zones and it seems to add years to life."

Red wine contains plant compounds such as resveratrol and flavonoids, which have been studied for their potential cardiovascular effects. However, experts have increasingly questioned whether any benefits attributed to red wine outweigh the known risks of alcohol.

Alcohol consumption has been linked to numerous health risks, including an increased risk of at least seven types of cancer, according to the U.S. Surgeon General.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People with underlying health conditions or those taking medications should consult a healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.
