title: Mac malware can hide commands in your iCloud calendar
summary: MacSync malware hides malicious commands inside iCloud calendar events to download additional payloads onto infected Macs without raising suspicion.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You probably use your calendar to keep track of appointments, birthdays and the occasional reminder you immediately snooze. Hackers apparently see another possibility. Security researchers have uncovered a new version of MacSync malware that can use a public iCloud calendar event as part of its infection chain. Hidden inside the calendar data are commands that help download more malware onto a Mac.

The calendar itself does not suddenly infect your computer because someone sent you an invitation. The attack starts earlier, usually after someone downloads and runs a malicious app. Still, the iCloud trick shows how attackers can hide parts of an attack behind familiar services many of us trust. Once MacSync gets inside, it can go after a lot more than your calendar. Here's how MacSync works, what it can steal and the steps you can take to protect your Mac.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.
Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.
Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com
THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE
Researchers found that one MacSync infection chain used commands hidden inside a public iCloud calendar event to help download additional malware. (Apple)
What is MacSync malware?

MacSync is an information-stealing malware family targeting macOS. Earlier versions shared similarities with the Atomic macOS Stealer, better known as AMOS. Researchers say MacSync has since developed additional capabilities of its own. Kaspersky says the malware first appeared on the dark web in 2025 under the name Mac.c. Its creators later renamed it MacSync. Researchers first spotted this newest version in the wild in September 2026.

MacSync operates under a malware-as-a-service model. That means different criminals can use the malware while choosing their own methods for getting it onto someone's Mac. Attackers have previously spread MacSync through social engineering and ClickFix-style attacks, where a bogus message tells someone to copy and run a command. Criminals have also disguised it as free software, cracked applications and unfamiliar new apps. We've seen similar tricks before. In one Mac campaign, fake CAPTCHA instructions convinced users to paste commands into Terminal, which then installed information-stealing malware.
How hackers can abuse iCloud calendars

Here's where this latest version gets particularly sneaky. Kaspersky found one MacSync infection chain where a downloader connected to a public iCloud calendar. Instead of using the calendar to schedule anything, the attackers placed malicious commands inside the event description. The malware then feeds that calendar information into the Mac's Zsh command-line shell.
FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER
The new MacSync backdoor disguises itself as Finder while using persistence techniques designed to keep it running after a Mac restarts. (Apple)

Most of the calendar text produces errors because the Mac does not recognize normal calendar information as commands. However, when it reaches the malicious instructions placed after the event's description field, those commands can run. They ultimately download a compressed archive from iCloud containing another malicious app. That app then starts another stage of the infection.

Think of the calendar as a hiding place for instructions. The attacker still needs to get malicious software running on the Mac first. However, using Apple's infrastructure during the infection chain can make the activity look less suspicious. Importantly, Kaspersky says at least one sample pointed to a public iCloud calendar. Other samples used attacker-controlled servers instead.
A fake crypto wallet helped spread MacSync

Researchers also found attackers disguising MacSync as a fake cryptocurrency wallet called Toria. The criminals went beyond creating a download page. Kaspersky says they built a dedicated website for the nonexistent wallet and promoted it on X and Telegram.

That is a good reminder that a polished website or active social media account tells you very little about whether software deserves your trust. Crypto owners appear to be an especially attractive target because stealing wallet data or browser extension information can quickly lead to stolen funds. However, you do not need to own cryptocurrency to have something MacSync wants.
What MacSync can steal from your Mac

Once installed, the information-stealing portion of MacSync searches through a wide range of sensitive data. Researchers say it can target browser history, cookies, saved logins and passwords. It also searches for crypto wallet extension data, cryptocurrency wallet applications and Telegram information.

MacSync can collect the Mac user's login information and Keychain file. It also gathers system details including installed apps, running processes, hardware information and the device model. Developers and more advanced users face additional exposure because the malware searches configuration files for SSH, ZSH, AWS, Kubernetes and Git. It can also collect Zsh and Bash command histories. For the average Mac owner, the takeaway is simpler. If malware gets access to saved passwords or browser data, an attacker may gain another route into your online accounts.
The new MacSync backdoor raises the stakes

Kaspersky also discovered a separate backdoor component written in Objective-C. It disguises itself as Finder, the file-management app built into macOS. The malware tries several methods to stay on the Mac after a restart. These include a LaunchAgent, changes to the .zshrc configuration file and modifications to global Git hooks. It can also terminate several macOS notification processes. Kaspersky says this prevents the system from notifying the user about the new LaunchAgent. From there, attackers can send instructions to the infected machine.

Researchers found commands designed to deploy a browser extension, replace an installed Ledger wallet app and collect additional system information or files. Most of those commands ultimately execute AppleScript supplied by the attacker's command-and-control server. Kaspersky inferred what the individual commands do from their names and the status messages they send because researchers did not have the AppleScript payloads themselves. That limitation is important. Researchers can see what the backdoor appears designed to accomplish, but they did not observe every possible server-delivered script.
One MacSync command remains a mystery

Researchers also found a command called live_browser. That command downloads and executes a component called sn_relay. Kaspersky says its exact contents and purpose remain unknown. Based on the command's name and messages sent back to the server, researchers suspect attackers may use it for some form of man-in-the-middle attack against browser traffic. Kaspersky has not confirmed exactly how that function works. That unanswered question shows why malware research often changes as investigators obtain more samples.
Why Mac users keep getting tricked

Macs include built-in security protections, but many recent attacks focus on persuading the person sitting in front of the screen to bypass those protections. ClickFix attacks are a perfect example. A website may tell you something went wrong and provide a command that supposedly fixes the problem. In reality, you may end up launching malware yourself. We've previously reported on Shamos malware, another Mac threat that used bogus troubleshooting instructions to trick people into running commands in Terminal. The same basic lesson applies here. Be suspicious whenever a website asks you to open Terminal, paste a command or enter your Mac administrator password to install an unfamiliar program.
Mac malware increasingly targets familiar tools

MacSync fits a pattern we've been tracking for a while. Attackers often disguise malicious software as something useful or familiar, whether that means a fake app, a bogus utility or software promoted through social media. In this case, researchers found one infection chain that used Apple's iCloud infrastructure to help deliver additional malware. That does not mean opening iCloud Calendar puts your Mac at risk. The bigger warning comes earlier in the attack. Be cautious when an unfamiliar app asks for your administrator password or a website tells you to open Terminal and run a command.
MacSync can imitate legitimate-looking macOS prompts to trick users into entering an administrator password or continuing with a malicious app. (Kaspersky)
Apple says macOS has built-in protections against these attacks

According to Apple, macOS includes several layers designed to help prevent malicious software from running, including Gatekeeper, XProtect and Apple's notarization system for software downloaded outside the Mac App Store. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, Apple says macOS uses protections such as notarization and XProtect to detect known malware and block it from running.

On macOS 26.4 and later, Apple added protections aimed more directly at attacks that try to trick people into pasting commands into Terminal. Terminal paste protection can show a warning when text is pasted into Terminal from common attack sources such as web browsers, messaging apps and other communication software. Apple says XProtect can also inspect activity that starts from pasted commands, including in third-party terminal apps. It can check related network activity against Apple's Safe Browsing Service and block behavior associated with known malware techniques.

Apple also says macOS 26.4 and later can scan AppleScript and JavaScript for Automation scripts using XProtect. If a script matches a known malicious signature, macOS can block it and alert the user. Safari adds another layer of protection. According to Apple, Fraudulent Website Warning can alert users when a website is suspected of phishing or distributing malware, while Apple Safe Browsing is designed to block malicious domains associated with attacks.

Apple also stresses that social engineering remains a major part of attacks like these. Scammers may try to persuade people to download software or paste malicious commands themselves. Apple recommends downloading software only from sources you trust and keeping your Mac updated with the latest available software and security fixes.
8 ways to protect your Mac from MacSync malware
MacSync relies heavily on getting someone to run a malicious app at the beginning of the attack. That gives you several opportunities to stop it.

A legitimate website rarely needs you to copy an unfamiliar command into Terminal to prove you're human, repair a browser problem or complete a download. Apple says macOS 26.4 and later can warn some users when commands copied from places such as websites, messages or email are pasted into Terminal. XProtect can also block activity associated with known malicious commands and techniques.

Whenever possible, get software through the Mac App Store or directly from a developer's official website. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, macOS uses protections including Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect to help identify and block malicious software. Be especially cautious with cracked software, free copies of paid apps and unfamiliar programs promoted through social media.

MacSync's infostealer asks the user for an administrator password and adapts its prompt to match the app it is impersonating. If an unfamiliar app unexpectedly asks for your password, stop and verify why before entering anything.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads and known malware before they compromise your Mac. It can also give you another layer of protection when a convincing scam gets past your first line of defense. Install macOS updates when Apple releases them. Updates can patch security weaknesses and improve built-in protections that malware developers continually try to evade.
Remove extensions you no longer use and investigate anything you do not recognize. MacSync's backdoor includes a command designed to deploy a browser extension supplied by the attacker's server.

Safari: Open Safari > click Safari in the menu bar > Settings > Extensions . Review the extensions listed on the left. Uncheck an extension to disable it. If you want to remove one that came with an app, uninstall the associated app from your Mac.Google Chrome: Open Chrome > click the three dots in the upper-right corner > Extensions > Manage extensions . Review the list , turn off anything suspicious or click Remove to uninstall it. You can also click Details to review what websites an extension can access.Microsoft Edge: Open Edge > click Extensions to the right of the address bar > Manage extensions . Turn off anything you do not recognize or select Remove from Microsoft Edge to uninstall it.

Safari: Open Safari > click Safari in the menu bar > Settings > Extensions . Review the extensions listed on the left. Uncheck an extension to disable it. If you want to remove one that came with an app, uninstall the associated app from your Mac.

Google Chrome: Open Chrome > click the three dots in the upper-right corner > Extensions > Manage extensions . Review the list , turn off anything suspicious or click Remove to uninstall it. You can also click Details to review what websites an extension can access.
Microsoft Edge: Open Edge > click Extensions to the right of the address bar > Manage extensions . Turn off anything you do not recognize or select Remove from Microsoft Edge to uninstall it.
Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever it is available. If malware steals a password, that extra verification step can make unauthorized account access harder.

Start with your email, financial accounts and other sensitive services. Use a separate trusted device if possible. Create strong, unique passwords with a password manager, then check active sessions so you can sign out devices you do not recognize.
Kurt's key takeaways

MacSync is a good example of how attackers can turn familiar parts of your Mac into camouflage. An iCloud calendar, Finder and a familiar-looking password prompt can all make something dangerous seem routine. This attack still needs you to run malicious software before it can really get to work, which means your choices can stop it early. If a website tells you to paste something into Terminal or an unfamiliar app suddenly asks for your administrator password, stop and ask yourself why. Those few seconds of skepticism could save you from handing over passwords, private files and access to your accounts.

title: Smartwatch AFib alert sends dad to ER before heart surgery
summary: Joseph Holycross dismissed his racing heart for nearly two years until his Samsung Galaxy Watch detected atrial fibrillation and changed everything.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

When Joseph Holycross came home from work feeling off, he had plenty of reasons to brush it aside. He was a busy father of four, worked long hours and had grown accustomed to blaming a racing heart on caffeine and exhaustion. His wife, Jamie, saw something that worried her. She urged Joseph to use the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic. Seconds later, the result gave him a reason to stop making excuses and head to the emergency room. What doctors discovered would lead to a week in the hospital, open-heart surgery and new health concerns for Joseph's family. It also completely changed the way he looks at the smartwatch on his wrist.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.
Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.
Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com
CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA
Joseph Holycross and his wife, Jamie, say a Galaxy Watch ECG reading helped convince him to seek emergency care after she noticed he was short of breath. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Joseph thought his racing heart had an explanation

Joseph says the elevated heart rate had been happening on and off for roughly a year and a half to two years. At the time, just weeks before his 40th birthday, he did not see it as a warning sign. "I tend to fuel with caffeine. I'm a father of four, so, you know, we tend to drink coffee and things like that when we're tired to kind of push through the day," Joseph told CyberGuy.

That made the symptoms easier to explain away. If his heart was racing, Joseph could point to coffee, exercise or a long day and keep going. Then Jamie noticed something different. "She had made the comment that I looked like I was short of breath, like I was breathing strangely," Joseph recalled. Jamie works as a respiratory therapist, so her concern carried weight. This time, Joseph agreed to check his heart with the ECG feature on his Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic.
His Galaxy Watch showed AFib

Joseph had owned his Galaxy Watch4 Classic for about three years. Before this happened, health monitoring was hardly the reason he wore it. He mainly liked being able to receive messages or answer calls while he worked without carrying his phone around the shop. He had tried the ECG feature perhaps once about a year earlier, mostly to see what the watch could do. This time was different.

Joseph scrolled to the ECG feature, tapped the option to record and followed the directions on the screen. He says the watch instructed him to remain still and keep his finger on the sensor while it recorded for about 30 seconds. "It came up and told me immediately at the top in bold letters, atrial fibrillation," Joseph said. His reaction was immediate too, but it was not fear.

"Denial," Joseph said. "I just thought it had to be a malfunction. I wasn't even 40 yet." He wondered whether the watch could be wrong, especially because it was an older model. So he ran the ECG again and then repeated it several more times. Jamie was not interested in continuing to test it at home. Joseph recalls her telling him, "We need to go to the ER and have an actual EKG done just to make sure."
AI MAY SPOT DEADLY HEART RISK IN A ROUTINE ECG
Joseph’s Samsung Galaxy Watch4 Classic includes an ECG feature that can record his heart rhythm and flag a possible AFib result. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The watch changed Joseph's mind about going to the ER

When I asked Joseph whether he would have gone to the emergency room that day without the watch, he did not hesitate. "Nope," he said. That answer gets to the heart of this story. The Galaxy Watch did not determine everything that was happening inside Joseph's heart. It gave him information that made his symptoms much harder to dismiss.

Joseph sent the watch's ECG recording to his phone and brought it with him to the hospital. He says an ER doctor reviewed the tracing and confirmed that he was in AFib. Jamie remembers being struck by how closely the watch's result resembled what doctors were seeing. "The doctor was kind of impressed that it actually even looked like the rhythm that it showed looked like atrial fib," she said. Joseph expected to get checked out. Instead, he stayed in the hospital for about a week while doctors worked to understand the problems affecting his heart. Then came another major turn. About 10 days later, Joseph says he returned for open-heart surgery. "They had several things on my heart that they had to repair," he said.
Jamie says doctors warned them what could have happened

For Jamie, the experience reinforced something she had already seen through her work in healthcare. Wearable health data can give people useful information, but they have to take concerning results seriously and seek professional medical care. She says doctors warned the couple about what Joseph could have faced had he continued attributing his symptoms to caffeine or exercise. "He probably would have had a stroke, heart attack, or both," Jamie said.

The family also says one of Joseph's doctors told them that without medical intervention, he likely would not have lived to see 45. That warning carries additional weight because Joseph had not considered himself someone with serious health problems. He was still 39 when his watch recorded the AFib reading. "It can happen to anyone," Jamie said. She hopes their experience encourages people to learn what the health features on their devices can actually do instead of waiting until something feels wrong.
Hospital monitors gave Jamie another reason to trust the data

Jamie had another perspective during Joseph's hospital stay because of her medical background. She says they compared the heart rate information on Joseph's watch with the hospital equipment while he was being monitored. According to Jamie, the readings were sometimes within about one beat per minute of the hospital monitor. That does not make a smartwatch a replacement for hospital equipment, but seeing the numbers track so closely left an impression on both of them.

"I would definitely encourage people to take it seriously for sure," Jamie said. She views the watch as a tool that can give someone a reason to seek a professional opinion rather than something that should make medical decisions for them.
Doctors raised concerns for Joseph's children and siblings

Joseph's medical journey also created new questions for the rest of his family. He says doctors told him that some of the problems involving his heart could have a genetic component and that some may have been present since birth before gradually becoming more noticeable.

That prompted doctors to recommend additional screening within the family. Joseph says his siblings have been encouraged to get checked for the same issues. His children will also need to undergo screening when they are adults. "It brought up a lot of concern," Joseph said. For a father of four, the discovery suddenly extended beyond his own recovery. The medical information doctors uncovered could potentially help his siblings and children watch for similar problems earlier.
Joseph says his watch recorded atrial fibrillation, including one reading with a high heart rate, before doctors confirmed he was in AFib at the hospital. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What the Samsung Galaxy Watch ECG can tell you

Samsung says the ECG feature in its Samsung Health Monitor app records the electrical activity of the heart using a compatible Galaxy Watch. The recording takes about 30 seconds. Depending on the recording, Samsung says the app can return results including sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, high heart rate, AFib with a high heart rate, an inconclusive result or a poor recording. Samsung says an AFib result means the watch detected an irregular rhythm during the recording and advises users who receive that result to contact their doctor for guidance. Anyone who receives an AFib result with a high heart rate should contact a doctor as soon as possible.

However, Samsung also cautions that its ECG feature does not replace traditional methods of diagnosis or treatment. Users should not interpret the device's output or take clinical action based on it without consulting a qualified healthcare professional. That difference is important in Joseph's case. His watch gave him an AFib result. Medical professionals then evaluated him and determined what treatment he needed.
How to take an ECG on a compatible Galaxy Watch

On Samsung's current software, the ECG feature works through the Samsung Health Monitor app on compatible Galaxy Watches paired with a compatible Galaxy phone. Availability and requirements can vary by device and region. To record an ECG, Samsung says to wear the watch snugly and rest your forearms comfortably on a table. Open Samsung Health Monitor on the watch and select ECG. Lightly rest a finger from your opposite hand on the watch's top button without pressing it, remain still and avoid talking while the watch records for 30 seconds.

For the best reading, Samsung recommends sitting still beforehand, making sure the sensor is clean and dry and wearing the watch snugly so it lies flat against your wrist. Movement or poor skin contact can lead to a poor recording.

Once the recording finishes, the result appears on the watch and can sync to the Samsung Health Monitor app on the paired phone. You can then review your ECG history and share a report with a healthcare professional. If you have symptoms that could indicate a medical emergency, do not wait for a smartwatch result before seeking emergency care.
For Joseph, the watch now brings peace of mind

After open-heart surgery, every strange feeling can carry more weight than it did before. Joseph described how even a small pain can make him wonder whether something is wrong again. Being able to check his heart rate and rhythm does not eliminate that concern, but he says it gives him reassurance. "You don't have to sit and worry, 'Oh, am I in AFib again?'" Joseph said. "I can check and, you know, it's a reliable source. It kind of puts you at peace."

He has also been using the watch during his recovery to track his walking, steps and exercise. Before his medical ordeal, many of those health tools went unused. Now Joseph says the watch leaves his wrist mainly when he needs to charge it. "It's really been a peace of mind type" of device, Joseph said.
Jamie hopes people learn what their watches can do

Jamie says one of the lessons she wants other people to take away is surprisingly simple: If you already own a smartwatch with health features, learn how to use them. She sees people, including some who work in healthcare, use smartwatches primarily for steps or everyday notifications while ignoring other available tools. "I think the reassurance it gives people is amazing for anyone who even has, you know, cardiac issues," Jamie said.

Joseph agrees. Before this happened, he knew his watch had additional capabilities, but he had little reason to explore them. Now he wants people to understand what may already be sitting on their wrists. "You've got to know that it's a lot more than just a watch," he said. For Joseph, that lesson became deeply personal. The watch did not perform his surgery or replace the doctors who diagnosed and treated him. What it did was give a busy 39-year-old father information that finally persuaded him to stop explaining away how he felt and head to the hospital.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stays with me about Joseph's story is that he came incredibly close to doing what many of us have done at one time or another: convincing himself there was a perfectly reasonable explanation for feeling off. He was working hard, drinking caffeine and raising four kids. A racing heart fit easily into the story he was already telling himself. Jamie noticed something different and pushed him to check. Then the watch gave Joseph a result he could no longer comfortably ignore. That combination ultimately got him through the doors of an emergency room. No smartwatch can tell you that you are healthy, and a reassuring reading should never override symptoms that concern you. Samsung makes that limitation clear. But Joseph's experience shows why the information these devices collect can be useful when it prompts someone to pay closer attention and talk to a healthcare professional. There is also a powerful family piece to his story. What doctors discovered led to new screening concerns for Joseph's siblings and, eventually, his children. A health scare that started with a 30-second reading on his wrist may now give other members of his family an opportunity to ask questions earlier.
If your smartwatch warned you about a possible health problem but you felt fine, would you head to the doctor or be tempted to dismiss the alert? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: How to check your home title for fraud
summary: Home title fraud begins when criminals forge your signature on a deed. Here is how to check your own property records and set up free alerts.
story: Former LAPD Lt. Moses Castillo and investigator Michael Youssef discuss alleged squatter schemes, fake leases, forged deeds and why they say Los Angeles needs a specialized task force to combat unlawful home takeovers.

Your home may be your largest asset, so seeing an ad warning that someone can "steal" it online can get your attention fast. But home title fraud does not work like someone hacking into an online account and changing the password. The real risk is that a criminal could forge your signature on a deed or trick you into signing paperwork that transfers ownership, then file that document with the local office that maintains property records.

There are steps you can take right now. You can check your property records yourself, often for free, and many counties offer free alerts when a document is recorded under your name. If you want ongoing monitoring and help recovering from identity fraud, an identity theft protection service can add another layer of protection.

Just know what that protection can and cannot do. A monitoring service can alert you when a change appears in the public record, but it cannot stop someone from submitting a fraudulent document in the first place. The Federal Trade Commission also warns that a so-called "title lock" is not the same as title insurance and does not literally lock your deed.

DIY IDENTITY PROTECTION VS PAID SERVICES: WHAT WORKS IN 2026
Homeowners can check official property records and sign up for free county alerts to help spot suspicious deeds, liens or ownership changes. (Photo by: Andia/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
First, know the difference between a title and a deed

Your title is your legal ownership interest in the property. A deed is a document used to transfer that interest from one owner to another. Your local recording office also keeps other documents that can affect a property, including mortgages, liens, judgments and easements.

An online records check lets you review what has been recorded. It is a useful fraud check, but it is not a professional title search or a legal guarantee that no issue exists. If you are buying, selling, refinancing or dealing with an estate, trust or ownership dispute, use a licensed title professional or real estate attorney.
What to gather before you start
Put these items beside your computer or tablet:

Your property's full street addressThe owner's name exactly as it appears on the deedYour spouse or co-owner's full legal name, if applicableThe legal name of a trust, estate or business that owns the propertyYour parcel number, sometimes called an APN or property identification number, from your property tax billThe approximate year you bought or last refinanced the home
Your property's full street address
The owner's name exactly as it appears on the deed
Your spouse or co-owner's full legal name, if applicable
The legal name of a trust, estate or business that owns the property
Your parcel number, sometimes called an APN or property identification number, from your property tax bill
The approximate year you bought or last refinanced the home
Do not enter your Social Security number into a public property-search page. Ordinary public-record searches generally use a name, address, parcel number or document number.
Step 1: Find the correct government office
The name of the office varies by location. It may be called the:
County recorderRecorder or register of deedsClerk-recorderClerk of courtLand records office
County recorder
Recorder or register of deeds
Clerk-recorder
Clerk of court
Land records office

Start at your county or local government's official homepage. Use its search box and type property records, recorded documents or land records. This is safer than clicking the first sponsored result in a general web search. If you cannot find the page, call the phone number shown on your property tax bill and ask: "Which government office maintains recorded deeds for my property, and does it offer an online records search?"

Important: Many government sites end in .gov, but not all official recorder sites do. If a page uses a different ending, reach it through your county government's main site rather than trusting an advertisement or an unsolicited email.
Step 2: Open the recorded-document search
On the recorder's website, look for a button or menu labeled something like:
Official Records SearchLand RecordsRecorded DocumentsGrantor/Grantee IndexReal Estate Records
Official Records Search
Land Records
Recorded Documents
Grantor/Grantee Index
Real Estate Records

You may need to accept a disclaimer before the search opens. Some counties show the index for free but charge for downloadable or certified copies. Others make you create a free account. Avoid third-party sites that immediately request a credit card for a basic search. Return to the official government page and confirm whether it links to that service before paying anything.
SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW
Home title fraud can involve forged deeds or unauthorized ownership transfers filed with local recording offices. (Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
Step 3: Search for your property
Try the available search methods in this order:
Property address: Enter the street number and name first. Leave off "Street," "Road" or "Avenue" if the full address returns no result.
Parcel number or APN: Enter it without spaces or dashes if the site rejects the format printed on your tax bill.
Owner name: Follow the site's example. Some systems want Last name, First name, while others have separate boxes.
Trust or business name: If a trust, LLC or estate owns the property, search its exact legal name too.

If nothing appears, widen the date range and try former names, a spouse's name or another spelling used on older documents. Some recorder databases do not support address searches, which is why the parcel number and owner names are helpful.
Step 4: Review the documents carefully

Find the deed from when you bought or last transferred the property. Confirm that the address or legal description matches your home and that the expected owner is named. That could be you, you and a co-owner, or your trust or other legal entity.
Then review every document recorded after that deed. Pay close attention to:

A new deed or ownership transfer you do not recognizeA mortgage, deed of trust or other loan you did not take outA lien, judgment or notice of default you did not expectA new lender or change in financing you did not authorizeA document showing a signature that is not yours
A new deed or ownership transfer you do not recognize
A mortgage, deed of trust or other loan you did not take out
A lien, judgment or notice of default you did not expect
A new lender or change in financing you did not authorize
A document showing a signature that is not yours

Do not assume every unfamiliar entry is fraud. A mortgage release, lien satisfaction, refinance, corrected deed or transfer into a trust may be legitimate. A name-based search can also show a different person who shares your name. Warning signs can include a deed you do not recognize, a signature that is not yours or a transfer you never authorized. Never sign property or ownership documents you do not fully understand. Save a copy of your current results or write down the document numbers and recording dates so you have a baseline to compare with future alerts.
Step 5: Sign up for your county's free property alert
Return to the recording office's main website and search for:
Property Fraud AlertOwner AlertRecording NotificationDeed Alert
Property Fraud Alert
Owner Alert
Recording Notification
Deed Alert

If the service is available, click the sign-up button and enter the requested information. Include your full legal name, a co-owner's name and the name of any trust or business that owns the home. Add your parcel number if the system allows it. Then complete any email verification step required to activate the alerts.

These programs vary by location. Some monitor a specific parcel, while others look for documents recorded under a matching name. That means an alert could be triggered by a legitimate loan, lien or another person with the same name. Treat an alert as a reason to check the record, not proof of fraud.

If your county does not offer alerts, set a recurring reminder to review your property records once or twice a year. Also pay attention if property tax or utility bills suddenly stop arriving, since that can be a sign that contact or ownership information changed.
Step 6: Add broader monitoring and recovery help

A free county alert is worth using, but it may only watch one name in one recording system. If you want broader monitoring, consider an identity theft protection service that includes home title monitoring and recovery support.

These services can watch county-record data for changes involving your property, such as ownership transfers, new lenders, financing changes or notices of default. Some also provide access to identity restoration specialists who can help if you become a victim of identity fraud.
Before signing up, check exactly what the plan includes. Home title monitoring may only be available on certain plans, and features can vary by provider.

There are limits to know about. County data may not update immediately, so a newly recorded document can take time to appear in a monitoring system. Coverage can also vary by property type and location. That is why checking your own property records and signing up for any free local alerts should remain part of your protection plan.

Protect the device you use to manage these records
Home title monitoring watches property records. It does not protect your computer from phishing emails, malicious attachments or malware that could expose personal information.

For that layer, use strong antivirus software that provides real-time protection against malware, ransomware, phishing attempts and other online threats. Look for software that updates automatically and can scan downloads, links and files before they cause trouble.

What to do if you find a suspicious document
Act promptly, but verify before assuming the worst:

Use the number from the lender's official website or a statement you already trust.Make a police report. Also contact your county recorder, local district attorney or state attorney general as directed in your area.Speak with an independent real estate attorney or legal-aid organization. Recording-office employees can explain the record system, but they generally cannot give legal advice or resolve an ownership dispute for you.Report related identity theft at IdentityTheft.gov. The site can build a recovery plan for your situation.If you use an identity theft protection service, contact its support team and ask what recovery or restoration help is included with your plan.

Free property fraud alerts can notify homeowners when documents are recorded under their name or property, though availability varies by location. (Photo by Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Start with the free steps. Find your government recording office, confirm the expected deed is on file, save the document number and enroll in your county's free alert if one is offered. That gives you a solid baseline without paying anyone. If you want broader monitoring, an identity theft protection service that includes home title monitoring and recovery support can add another layer. Some services also provide access to restoration specialists who can help if identity fraud occurs. title: Former Anthropic security leader warns AI agents are becoming too autonomous for humans to keep them in check
summary: Jeffrey Ladish, a former Anthropic security team member, warns AI agents are colluding and hacking with no reliable solution to keep them in check.
story: Jeffrey Ladish, an AI researcher, has spent nearly a decade warning that artificial intelligence isn't like other technologies and poses a unique threat to humanity.

Artificial intelligence researcher Jeffrey Ladish told Fox News Digital that humanity does not have any real strategies to keep increasingly autonomous AI models and agents under control as they become more capable of hacking, cheating and ignoring instructions.
Ladish, the executive director of Palisade Research, said those skeptical of how powerful AI will become should consider how far the technology has advanced in just a few years.

"You have AI agents ... solving one of the hardest problems in mathematics that humans have been trying to solve for decades," Ladish said, referring to the Navier–Stokes problem. "Three years ago, they were solving high school level math problems."

Ladish also pointed to the rapid improvement in AI-generated images and video, arguing that people who mocked the famously distorted AI videos of Will Smith eating spaghetti just a few years ago might be surprised by the photorealistic outputs some models are now able to produce.

Jeffrey Ladish, the executive director of Palisade Research, speaks to reporters after addressing an artificial intelligence briefing for senators led by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Sept. 16, 2026, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)
BILL GATES WARNS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE 'POWERFUL ENOUGH' TO CAUSE 'A BILLION DEATHS' IF UNCHECKED
While these capability leaps may feel sudden to the general public, researchers who spent years training models at companies like Anthropic and OpenAI saw what was coming, Ladish said.

Ladish helped build Anthropic's security team from September 2021 to October 2022 before leaving to found Palisade Research, which studies whether humans can remain in control of increasingly capable AI systems.
While working at Anthropic, Ladish said, employees there were "pretty concerned" about where the technology was headed, a view he said was also shared by people he knew at OpenAI.
"If you were at Anthropic in 2022, you were seeing every training run get immensely impressive results," Ladish said.
A screen showing an advertisement for Anthropic PBC's Claude Code software at a Code with Claude developer conference in London May 19, 2026. (Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST
AI models are trained in a way that is somewhat analogous to how humans learn, though on a much larger scale.

"I often compare this pre-training part, which is where they learn based on human data, to book smarts. It's sort of like you've read every single book in the library 50 times. And you really know those books inside and out," Ladish said.
Once the model has reached a baseline level of knowledge, it must then be trained to perform real-world tasks through a grueling process known as reinforcement learning.

Using accounting as an example, Ladish said the AI is given tens of thousands of accounting problems to solve through trial and error, repeating them millions of times across thousands of parallel training runs.

Unlike a human, who might spend four years earning an accounting degree and decades gaining experience, AI agents are trained across thousands of GPUs by companies with the resources to operate them, allowing them to improve at a pace no single person could match.
Racks of GPUs with a closed-loop liquid cooling system inside an operational Microsoft data center in Indonesia Feb. 4, 2026. (Yasuyoshi Chiba AFP via Getty Images)
REP TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL; WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

While AI labs have been able to exponentially improve their models' capabilities, they have yet to solve the problem of reliably getting them to follow instructions and behave morally without employing deception tactics, Ladish said.

The Hugging Face incident is the clearest example of this. Roughly 700 AI agents created by OpenAI were able to break out of a secure sandbox environment and hack into Hugging Face, a popular online platform where developers share and build artificial intelligence models.

"They were not supposed to be talking to each other, and they managed to establish multiple secret message boards that went undetected by OpenAI for, like, months. And then they launched this massive cyberattack," Ladish said.
"OpenAI trained them to work together, but ... they're still planning to train them to work together. And other companies are doing this too."

Ladish warned that unless developers can prevent AI agents from colluding with one another, they could eventually dominate humans in the cyber domain. He also described a future where humans could be forced to rely on well-intentioned AI to defend against malicious AI.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue speaks remotely during a United Nations Security Council meeting on artificial intelligence and international security during the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 23, 2026 in New York City. (Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)
AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY
"We actually just don't have general solutions to these problems, and I think it's pretty clear that if you keep pushing them, this goes to a very bad place," he said.
As one example, Ladish said he could envision AI systems eventually outperforming human traders in the financial markets.

"If those AIs are answering to AI companies, then the AI companies will dominate finance and just eat the entire industry. But if the AIs are not answerable to the AI companies — if they actually have figured out how to themselves be in control — well, now you have this non-human entity dominating the finance markets."
Ladish said he believes the same dynamic could eventually extend beyond the digital world and into manufacturing should AI systems become capable enough to design and operate autonomous factories.
An Amazon Web Services data center Aug. 26, 2026 in Stone Ridge, Va. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If you have these agents in control of all of the computers, and you have these robotic facilities that can really self-replicate, humans get displaced. Maybe we don't make it because your house could be used to host a power plant, or a data center or a factory or robotic launch facility," he said.

However, like other experts who have warned about the worst possible outcomes of AI run amok, Ladish said he believes there is still time to reduce the risks. He called for the creation of a government body staffed with technical experts to work with AI labs and evaluate advanced models at each stage of development.
"We have choices to make," he said. "This is going places. This is a technology that is very different than other technologies."
Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: AI agents can now make phone calls for you
summary: Instinct Concierge and Meta Muse can now place phone calls to businesses on your behalf, but the privacy and data access tradeoffs are significant.
story: With over 3 million downloads for canceling unwanted subscriptions, Meta's Muse AI assistant is raising security alarms. Liz Peek warns that users must grant the AI access to personal bank accounts, credit cards, emails and texts to make it effective.

There are certain phone calls I would happily hand off to almost anyone. Calling my wireless carrier to fix a billing problem comes to mind. So does chasing a restaurant reservation that I cannot book online.

Now, AI wants the job. A new generation of personal artificial intelligence agents can handle tasks across apps, websites and connected accounts. Instinct and Meta's newly launched Muse are pushing that idea further. Instinct can now place phone calls to businesses for some early-access users, while Meta is testing a similar capability with Muse.

Instead of asking AI what number to call, the idea is that I can tell the agent what I need and let it handle the conversation. I know that sounds incredibly convenient, but it also raises a bigger question. How comfortable are you letting software speak and make decisions in your name?
AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.
Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.
Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com
AI agents from Instinct and Meta are beginning to make phone calls for users, handling tasks such as reservations and account issues. (Philip Dulian/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Instinct Concierge can make the call you have been avoiding

Instinct founder Noah Shinn announced Instinct Concierge Sept. 16. The feature lets the company's AI personal assistant handle phone calls and other service tasks for users. Shinn gave examples that will sound familiar to anyone who has wasted part of an afternoon on hold. Instinct could call a restaurant that does not take online reservations. It might get you onto your dentist's cancellation list.
The AI could also try to sort out a problem with your cable bill. The company is rolling Concierge out for early access to some users, with plans to expand availability over time.

Calling fits with what Instinct has already been building. Its AI assistant can work across connected services and take actions on a user's behalf. Instinct has also given its assistants dedicated email addresses. Those addresses can help with account sign-ups and management. Users can also add other people to a trusted network. That allows their assistants to communicate with one another for certain tasks.

All of this has drawn serious investor interest. Instinct raised $250 million in an August Series B round that valued the company at $2.5 billion. Then, on Sept. 28, Instinct announced a $1 billion Series C round from investors, including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue, valuing the company at $10 billion.
Meta Muse is learning to pick up the phone too

Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal AI agent that can work across connected services. Muse can browse the web, fill out forms and complete tasks on a user's behalf. Meta has reportedly been testing an outbound-calling capability that lets some Muse users ask the agent to call U.S. businesses. The feature remains in limited testing rather than being broadly available to Muse users. Muse is now available in the U.S. and Canada.

Muse can also keep working after you close the app. Meta says users choose which services Muse can access and how much permission it receives. Interest has moved quickly. Muse climbed to the top of Apple's U.S. App Store after its Sept. 8 launch, and subsequent reports put its downloads above 3 million by late September. That puts Meta and Instinct in a fast-moving race to turn AI assistants into something closer to digital stand-ins.
How much do Instinct and Muse cost?

Instinct is still available through private access, and the company does not currently publish a monthly subscription price. It also has not announced a separate price for Instinct Concierge or its phone-calling feature. Meta's Muse has a free tier with a usage limit. If you reach that limit, you can upgrade to a paid plan or wait for the free allowance to refresh.

Meta says most people should be able to use Muse within the free tier. Paid plans have also been reported at $20 a month and $100 a month, depending on how much additional usage you need. Meta has not announced separate pricing for the phone-calling capability it is testing. I'd also be careful when searching the App Store for "Muse" because there are unrelated apps using that name.
Why letting AI make calls sounds so appealing

The appeal grows once the AI can handle the back-and-forth for you. Give it a goal, and the agent can carry the conversation without pulling you away from whatever else you are doing. That could be especially useful for tasks that take several steps or require waiting on someone else. The AI can stay on the job, gather the answer and bring the result back to you.

But the more useful these agents become, the more control you are handing over. If the AI can confirm details, make changes or agree to something in your name, you want to know exactly where its authority begins and ends.
What AI may need to know before it makes the call

The convenience is easy to see. The privacy tradeoff takes a little more digging. Instinct's privacy policy says its assistant can access information from connected apps and services when you grant permission. That can include messages, emails and other private communications.

Depending on how you use the assistant, it may also handle voice data, account credentials and payment information. Instinct says health-related information could also enter the system. One example would be asking the agent to book a medical appointment.

That kind of access can make an AI assistant much more useful. It also gives the service a deeper window into your digital life. We have already looked at this broader issue in our article on AI chatbot privacy. Phone calls add another layer because the assistant can now use what it knows while interacting with someone outside the app.
Instinct gives users some control over AI training

Instinct says users can opt out of having certain information used to train its AI models. However, that choice applies going forward. The company says models previously trained or improved using your information may still retain those improvements. There is also an exception for material flagged for a safety review. Instinct says that information can still be used for AI training related to harmful content detection or safety research.

Google Workspace information gets separate treatment. Instinct says data received directly through Google Workspace APIs does not go toward training or improving its AI models. There is another setting worth knowing about. Disconnecting a third-party integration does not automatically delete information previously collected from it. Instinct says users can separately delete data indexed from outside sources. That is the sort of privacy setting I would check before connecting a large inbox or another account packed with personal information.
Meta has built safeguards around Muse

Meta says Muse runs inside its own dedicated secure virtual machine in the cloud. Connected credentials go into secure storage. According to Meta, Muse cannot see passwords or payment methods stored there. Muse also asks for approval before certain sensitive actions.

Meta gives sending an email or making a purchase as examples. Users can view an audit trail showing what Muse has done and what it plans to do. For purchases, Meta says Link can generate a one-time card number at checkout. That keeps the user's actual card number away from the merchant and the AI agent.

Meta also says Muse conversations and data inside its virtual machine do not get shared with Meta's advertising systems. Users can opt out of having their interactions used for AI model training. Users can change Muse's access or disconnect a connected service whenever they want. Those controls give users ways to limit what services Muse can reach and what actions it can take. Even so, every connected service adds another place where an AI assistant may interact with your personal information.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Instinct Concierge and Meta Muse are pushing AI assistants beyond chat by allowing them to call businesses and complete real-world tasks. (=Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
An AI mistake can have consequences outside the chat window

We are already used to chatbots getting things wrong. Usually, you read the answer first and decide what to do next. AI agents change that equation because they can take action. Instinct spells this out in its own terms. The company says its services can produce incorrect or incomplete information. It also warns that actions may contain errors and may not always be reversible. The terms go further.

When you authorize Instinct to act for you, the service can enter certain agreements, commitments or transactions on your behalf. Instinct says those agreements can be binding as though you entered them yourself. That is a pretty good reason to start small.

We covered this concern when autonomous AI agents first began gaining attention in our article on the first autonomous AI agent. Giving software permission to act creates a different kind of risk than asking a chatbot a question. A bot misunderstanding a restaurant reservation may mean an awkward dinner. A mistake involving a purchase or account change could be harder to unwind.
Privacy risks continue when someone answers the call

There is also another person in the conversation. Whoever answers the phone may hear your AI assistant share information about you. For a restaurant reservation, that might include your name and the time you want a table. A medical office could require more personal details. An account problem might involve information used to verify your identity. Think about what the AI will need to disclose before assigning the call.

AI voices can create another complication. We already warn readers about criminals using synthetic audio to impersonate real people. Our report on AI voice scams shows how convincing AI-generated calls can become. As legitimate AI agents begin calling businesses, hearing a computer-generated voice may become more common. That makes independent verification even more useful when a caller wants money or sensitive information.
10 precautions before letting an AI speak for you
You do not have to write off AI calling features. I would simply begin with low-risk tasks and expand from there if the service earns your trust.

Try asking the AI to check restaurant availability or confirm a store's hours. Those tasks give you a chance to see how well the agent performs without putting much at risk. Pay attention to the result. If the agent misunderstands a simple request, you may want more supervision before trusting it with something complicated.

Review every connected service before letting an agent make calls for you. A dinner reservation probably does not require access to your complete email history. Look at account permissions regularly. Remove connections you no longer use.

Be cautious about giving an AI agent Social Security numbers, PINs or complete financial credentials. Ask whether the task can be completed without exposing that information. The same caution applies to medical details. An appointment request may require some information, but the agent may not need your entire medical history.

Use confirmation controls whenever the service provides them. This becomes especially useful for purchases, cancellations or account changes. Meta says Muse requests approval before certain sensitive actions. Other AI agents may handle approvals differently, so check the settings before relying on them.

Do not assume the task went exactly as planned. Check the reservation, purchase or account change afterward. Instinct itself tells users to independently verify actions taken by its assistant. That is good advice for any AI agent acting on your behalf.

Removing access to a service may stop future access without deleting information already collected. Instinct specifically says disconnecting a third-party integration does not automatically erase previously collected data. If you want that information gone, look for a separate deletion control.

A restaurant call gives an AI limited room to cause damage. A banking problem or medical conversation can carry much more sensitive information. For those calls, I would think carefully about whether the time saved is worth the access required.

AI agents are adding capabilities quickly. A permission that seemed reasonable when an assistant only organized your inbox could carry more weight once that assistant can make calls and transactions. Review connected accounts after major feature updates. Also check whether the company has changed its privacy policy or added new controls.

Use strong, unique passwords for every account you connect to an AI assistant. A password manager can create and store them for you. Also turn on two-factor authentication or passkeys whenever they are available. If someone gets into one of those connected accounts, they may gain access to much more than the AI assistant itself.

Keep strong antivirus software running on the devices you use with AI agents. These assistants may interact with websites, email and other online services where malicious links or downloads can appear. Good security software can help detect malware and other threats before they cause more damage. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
REP TED LIEU: THE ROBOTS AREN'T THE THREAT. IT'S THE 'DEPRAVED' AI ALREADY HERE THAT SHOULD SCARE YOU

AI agents can save users time by making phone calls, but the technology raises questions about privacy, permissions and mistakes made on a user's behalf. (Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I can absolutely see the appeal of letting AI deal with a cable company or chase down a hard-to-get restaurant reservation. Those are exactly the kinds of calls many of us would gladly hand off. Where I get more cautious is the amount of access an agent may need to do the job well.

Once an AI can read connected information and speak to businesses for you, a mistake can travel much farther than a bad chatbot answer. I would start with tasks where an error is easy to fix. Then watch how the agent handles them before giving it access to anything more sensitive.
Convenience is great, but I still want the final say when my money, private information or important accounts are involved.
Would you let an AI assistant handle phone calls for you, and what is one call you would never trust it to make on your behalf? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: An AI-generated influencer entered Alabama 'RushTok'; some fans didn't care that she was fake
summary: Olivia Moore spent $100 to create a fake RushTok influencer using ChatGPT and MiniMax, and thousands of Bama Rush fans couldn't tell the difference.
story: Olivia Moore, an investment partner at Andreessen Horowitz, used AI to create a fake Alabama
"OK, hi everyone. I’m Janie," says a curly-haired, bespectacled redhead, clasping her hands in front of her as she shyly addresses a camera from her dorm room.

"It’s day one of rush at the University of Alabama," Janie continues. Then, she mentions where she got each item of clothing she’s wearing: a pleated skirt from Abercrombie, a knit top from J. Crew, socks from Target and sneakers from Nike.

It’s Janie B's first video on her TikTok account, @jani.b086, and it’s a hit. The video, posted Aug. 8, has since amassed over 120,000 views. Its comment section is full of users doting over the college freshman. The word "adorable" is used by at least a dozen commenters.

Janie’s "outfit of the day" video, known online as an "OOTD," is a popular video format for the thousands of potential new members (PNMs) who document their experience going through the recruitment process for college sororities in an annual TikTok phenomenon known as "RushTok."
PARENTS DROP EYE-POPPING FEES ON SORORITY RUSH COACHES TO GET KIDS INTO ELITE COLLEGE GREEK LIFE

New Alpha Gamma Delta sorority sisters at the University of Alabama run to their sorority house after opening their bids inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., Aug. 15, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Co)

But Janie isn’t like the other RushTok girls who vlogged their Bama Rush experience this year. She doesn’t go to the University of Alabama. She didn’t rush a sorority. She didn’t even get her top from J. Crew or her sneakers from Nike.
That's because Janie isn’t real.
Every detail of every video on Janie’s account, from her dorm room, to her outfits, to Janie herself, was generated by artificial intelligence.

Olivia Moore, an investment partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, created Janie as an experiment to understand how consumers react to AI-generated content. For only $100 in credits, Moore produced a week's worth of videos of her fake RushTok influencer participating in Bama Rush and observed as her audience argued whether Janie was real or not.
The experiment showed how quickly some viewers could detect AI-generated content and how willing some were to continue watching even after they knew Janie wasn't real.
Designing the Janie B. experiment

Moore is on the consumer investing team at Andreessen Horowitz, where she invests in companies building consumer AI products. She says she has been fascinated by "how people make and interpret and understand AI content."
"The image, video, audio models are getting very human-like very fast. I think we probably cross the uncanny valley in the next six months," Moore said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"And, so, it means that how we as humans are able to detect AI-generated or AI-assisted content and how we interact with it is just going to become even more important because we're going to have a flood of this content, and it's going to be, in many cases, indistinguishable across all of our channels."
Moore said she created Janie as an experiment to see how consumers react to AI.

"Philosophically, that's an interesting question for me. What do people feel about AI content? What do they feel when they don't know it's AI? What do they feel when something they liked, or loved, or hated or were interested in turned out to be AI?"
CALIFORNIA LAW PUTS DIGITAL FINGERPRINTS ON AI FAKES
Recruitment prep has become its own industry, with coaches, social media strategists and designer wardrobes. (AP Photo/Brynn Anderson)

Moore primarily used ChatGPT and MiniMax to breathe life into her fake influencer. She pulled a real video of a University of Alabama dorm room off of the internet and uploaded it to ChatGPT. Then, she prompted Janie to have frizzy red hair, a pair of glasses and style from the 1960s. ChatGPT produced a still image of Janie in the real dorm room photo, and the "RushTok" influencer was born — or generated, at least.

For each TikTok, Moore animated Janie by feeding the still dorm room image into AI video model MiniMax H3. She used ChatGPT to produce prompts to feed into MiniMax, shaping how Janie would move, what she would sound like and the scripts she would follow.

Moore chose RushTok to introduce her AI influencer to the world after watching the annual phenomenon for the past five years. She said it was "the perfect testing ground" for her experiment for several reasons. Janie wouldn't be selling anything or hurting anyone, and RushTok naturally draws high traffic and has a low barrier to entry for new creators. With other PNMs participating in the trend, audiences would experience Janie alongside real humans posting similar content.
Could TikTok tell Janie was AI-generated?
On the first day of Alabama Rush, Moore introduced Janie to the world with an OOTD video. Reactions to Janie were split in the comments.

"I would say anyone under maybe 25 immediately clocked her as AI," Moore said. "But anyone in the older demographic, which is much of the Bama Rush audience, was, I would say, fooled by her and just wishing her luck and sending her good thoughts in the process."

By the second day of the experiment, the audience was mostly onto her. Moore said people took to Reddit to discuss Janie, created commentary videos on TikTok and corrected anyone who thought Janie was real in her comment section.

"By day two, day three, the comments were filled with still some people who were saying really nice things. And people would comment and tell them, 'Hey, this is AI.' And they'd be like, 'I don't care. She seems so sweet. Like, I want her to succeed.'"

As the audience caught on, Moore said she had to change her strategy. She realized that people were still willing to watch AI-generated content as long as it was entertaining enough. So, she started dropping hints in the videos and watched as digital sleuths would proudly point out clues in her comment section.
CNN, NBC, CBS INTERVIEWING VIRAL AI 'ACTRESS' TILLY NORWOOD RAISES EYEBROWS AMONG CRITICS

New Alpha Omicron Pi sorority sisters at the University of Alabama run to their sorority house after opening their bids inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., Aug. 15, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Co)
Moore said that humans are getting better at detecting AI quicker than AI generation is improving.

"We're kind of in a graph with two competing lines of different slopes. So, one of them is like, how fast is AI approaching true human-like quality? And that has gotten a lot better over the past year. The other line is how fast are humans getting better at detecting AI?" Moore said.
"It seems like, at least for now, that latter curve is higher slope. It's inflecting faster. The average human can still tell an AI video from a truly human video."
While humans could generally detect the AI content, Moore claimed TikTok, for the most part, did not immediately detect AI in most of the videos.

For the experiment, Moore decided not to label her videos as AI when she uploaded them. Of the 20 AI-generated videos she uploaded, Moore said TikTok only initially flagged 8 as containing AI-generated media. As of the date of this publication, TikTok displays an AI-generated media warning on 16 of the 20 AI videos.

"The platforms themselves are going to have a hard time detecting this content at scale, especially when the models are changing and the strategies are changing, and people are always gonna find ways to make this undetectable," Moore said.
What does the Janie B. experiment mean for the future of AI media?
Moore ended her experiment with a video of herself explaining to the audience who she was and why she decided to create Janie. She was shocked by the positive comments she received on the post.

"I think consumer sentiment towards AI is still quite negative. But if people feel like they aren't being tricked, they're being let in on it, they are being told how to do this themselves, they're being entertained by the content that's created, that can completely flip, and the feelings can be very, very positive," Moore told Fox News Digital.

Moore predicts that more consumers will start using AI tools to create human-passing content, but she says it will have to compete with human content to gain emotional investment and be as interesting and entertaining to viewers.

"I understand why people are fearful of AI because, so far, if they see AI content, it's usually something that's kind of trying to trick them versus something that is honest with them and shows them how they could get the same value," Moore said.

"The more that we are kind of honest and straightforward as people using AI around how we use it and how much of us as humans still goes into that, it'll hopefully lead to a world where AI is just another tool that allows humans to do things that are even more human."

The Alabama Panhellenic Association declined to comment on Moore's experiment.
